speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 38, to amend the Immigration Act.	'

subtopic: IMMIGRATION OFFICERS TO GET FREE TRANSPORTATION ON TRAINS.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
subtopic: IMMIGRATION OFFICERS TO GET FREE TRANSPORTATION ON TRAINS.
speechtext:
The Bill is a very short one. It contains only one section,. providing that transportation companies shall furnish free to immigration officers such transportation as is necessary to enable them to carry on their duties. It will be remembered that last session a provision was inserted in the Railway 'Act doing away with passes. Now we have along the border from the Atlantic to the Pacific a large number of immigration officers whose duties require them to travel upon trains practically every day, and unless we make the necessary provision the Government will have to pay fox their transportation.

A sijnilar provision td the one now proposed is contained in the Customs Act with respect to customs officials.

subsubtopic: PREMATURE DISCLOSURE OP INFORMATION.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct the attention -of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization to some reports appearing in the press this morning in respect of the report of the committee of which he is chairman. I desire to ask him if his report has yet been tabled and, if not, when will it be brought down? Further, I would ask him how it is that very important sections of his supposed report have reached the public press before the report itself has been submitted to the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
subsubtopic: PREMATURE DISCLOSURE OP INFORMATION.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has as much information as I have as to the manner in which the report which appeared in the press this morning got there. As a matter of fact, every member of the committee is very much disturbed by the fact that in some way or other some of the recommendations which we have been considering have reached the press. We are having a meeting of the committee this afternoon at half past three or four o'clock when doubtless the matter will be considered, and it is possible that some action may have to be taken in connection with the disclosure. The committee has not yet reached its final finding. We have one more meeting before our report will have been finally approved. That meeting will be held this afternoon, and any representations that are made to the press by any one until our report is finally reached are consequently without any accredited foundation. We have gone over all our work and have tentatively reached our finding. The whole matter is in the hands of the press, and if the printing can be finished we expect to have the report ready for presentation to the House probably this evening or at least to-morrow. It seems to me that the House should take cognizance of the fact that some of the committee's recommend,ations which were . under consideration have been obtained by some means and used by one of the papers in the city as practically intimating what our findings are before they have been absolutely settled by the committee.

subsubtopic: PREMATURE DISCLOSURE OP INFORMATION.
speechtext:

Mr. CALDEtR: I hardly feel called upon at the present time to give any such assurance, but I certainly think that the matter is worthy of consideration by the committee, and probably subsequently by the House itself.

speechtext: I cannot see very much in the argument of the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). He takes issue with the Government as to really owning the Grand Trunk so long as we do not take over the guaranteed stock and pay for it. There is no doubt that the holders of the guaranteed stock would be very glad if we would pay them the money now and take the stock Over. I do not believe that this, or any future, Government will want to take over this stock within thirty years, or for years afterwards, so long as they can get the money at four per cent. If we were to purchase the stock now we would have to borrow.money at 5J or 6 per cent. But we have shorn this stock of some of its value to the shareholders by reason of having taken away the voting power, placing it merely as a liability and allowing them to hold the stock as security for the guarantee given by the Government. I do not think it would be at all serious if we leave it as it is. We thought it was in our interest to have a limit, but that the period should be an extended one when the money was invested at so low a rate of interest. I cannot see that it will be any advantage to the Government to take over the stock before that time. I do not see that it affects public ownership for the reason that all the other stock, the first, second and third preference and the common stock, is transferred to the Government. We have $180,000,000 worth of scrip handed over in the vault. Out of $240,000,000, we have $180,000,000 and they still hold $60,000,000 worth of scrip without any voting powers as security for the guarantee. I cannot see any advantage in the amendment of the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I always understoood '
that you could only get rid of a liability and stop paying dividends when you paid the money for the stock you were getting. Therefore those who borrow the money in the future to pay for this stock will have to pay interest upon it. The statement was made last evening by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that this stock was al( water. I made inquiries in refer-

ence to this stock. For the greater portion of it the public paid par and the money all went into the road.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I admitted that in regard to the guaranteed stock. The common stock was the stock that I referred to as being nearly all water. It is not all water, because the minister has shown that $30,000,000 was paid on the common stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Perhaps it would not be any harm to tell the committee that for the larger portion of the $60,000,000 of guaranteed stock they paid par, for another portion ninety-eight, and for a small portion ninety-five, at the time it was issued. For all the stock that we are talking about now the people in England practically paid par.
Therefore, any person holding any idea different from that is wrong in his view. With reference to the purchasing of the stock at the present time we all know it would be absurd for the Government, or any person, to go on the market now and purchase the stock at whatever figure it is quoted at. There might be a little stock on the market that some person must sell, and it is owing to the high rate of interest that the stock is lower than it would be in normal times. But let me say to the hon. gentleman that prior to the war this stock was selling at from, I think, about 95 to 105. When times improve and money becomes cheaper, as the hon. gentleman suggests, up will go the price of this stock. I believe that when times again become normal this stock will likely go above par and that is the reason we wish to purchase at par. By doing so we will protect ourselves to that extent, and if interest rates drop the price of the stock will of course rise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Why fix a
time which prevents you from making the purchase within thirty years? Why not reserve to the Government the right to make the purchase at any time it is obviously apparent they should make it?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
This is practically a
bond and there should be a time limit on it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Why?
Mr. J. D. REIDi We do not sell bonds on the understanding that we can take them up at any time. They must be held for a certain time and the period of 30 years is the period that was agreed upon.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The question of watered stock is an interesting one in its place; the question of the market value of these stocks is also an interesting one in its place; but

neither of these questions is concerned in the present clause or in the amendment before the House. I entirely agree with the hon. gentleman that it would not be wise for us to buy this stock now at par, and I do not want to enter again into the question of its market value, but here is the situation: The minister is preceding on the assumption that we are asking that the stock shall be taken over by the Government at some particular early time, and that that is the motion of the hon. member from Prince. The Minister of Railways says that money just now is worth more than four per cent. Certainly, we have no inducement to buy the stock at the present moment; but money may be worth less than four per cent within a much shorter period than thirty years. If the war has depreciated the value of securities or enhanced the rate of interest on money, that is not a condition that is going' to be enduring. We have borrowed money before the war at three per cent and three and a quarter per cent; and in the happy days of another government we borrowed money at two and three-quarters per cent. I do not think we are going to have an immediate return to these rates, but it is not unreasonable to suppose that in much less than thirty years the Government of Canada will be able to borrow money at less than four per cent; and if at any time, no matter when it may occur, that happy condition of the market arises, why should we keep on paying four per cent to these people when money is only worth three or three and a half per cent? We are not, by this amendment, asking that the Government shall at any particular time be obliged to take this stock; we simply say the Government shall have the option to take it. If it does not suit them to take it to-day it may suit them to take it next year, or five or ten years hence. Then why in the world should we say, no matter what may be the improved condition of the money market, we are going to continue to pay four per cent on this stock for a period of thirty years? I think the argument of my hon. friend is based on a misconception, and he ought to support this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
himself does not support it because the amendment itself does not say we shall redeem the stock in five, ten, or twenty years ; if it did it would be more reasonable. The hon. gentleman should remember that this stock is perpetual stock that never matures; it also has voting power. The shareholders are being asked, first, to give up the voting power-a point we have already discussed.
\

In the second place, they are being asked to give up the perpetual character of the stock and to give us the option of redeeming it. The reason thirty years was fixed was that it was felt to be highly improbable that we could look for a lower rate than four per cent money within that time owing to the state of the world to-day and the tremendous obligations that all countries and all money markets are under. Furthermore, a bond must be a bond; it is wholly unreasonable to ask people to put their bonds into such a position that they cease to be bonds at all. If a bond is to be redeemable at any time then, as the hon. member will see at a glance, that takes it out of the category of bonds altogether- it is something wholly unknown in the markets so far as I have any knowledge of it, and so far as the hon. gentleman has. It might be-I do not think I am very much of a judge; I do not think that anybody is just now-it might be possible that it would pay the Government to redeem inside of thirty years. It might he possible that there would come a period within that time that it would be fair to do so if the Government have an opportunity of redeeming, providing a fixed time were allowed so that the bond would still remain a bond, or a security, of the character it is intended it shall be, and not a mere fleeting document that could be taken-up at any time and consequently be unsaleable. It might be wise that the thirty years should be limited-I do not know whether there would be any difficulty in arranging that or not, I should not presume there would be; but I think the hon. gentleman, if he is apprehensive that money will be less than four per cent before thirty years, will agree that the right way to go about it is to reduce that thirty years to a shorter term. I think it would be wholly unreasonable to simply leave the matter in such a state that no one would know that he would have his bond or that he would have his money.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
There is only one sense in which this can be called a bond-in the sense that we are taking a weak security and giving it the character of a government guarantee. In that way, you can call it a bond; however, I do not want to enlarge on that aspect of the question. There is nothing unusual in issuing bonds to run for thirty years with a right to call them in in less than that time. In that case you are engaging in a transaction, you are offering something to the public and inducing them to buy, and you have to make your
terms as attractive as you can. That is not the case here. We are not offering something to the public and trying to coax them to buy it. We are being coaxed to buy at par stock which is only worth 45 or 50. I cannot see any reason in the world why we should not have the absolute option of redeeming this stock at any time. Surely, if we are going to take stock which is worth a very low figure to-day and to take upon ourselves the obligation either to pay four per cent in perpetuity or redeem it, we [DOT] ought to have the right to redeem it at any time that it suits us. There is, however, sufficient force in the point for me to say it would be unwise to tie the hands of the arbitrators in that regard.
As to fixing a maximum award, I need scarcely say that matter has received very serious consideration. A great deal can be said on each side of the question. The presence of a maximum is argued by some as being in the nature of an indication to the board of arbitration as to what the country would stand for, as to what might be awarded without serious complaint. On the other hand, the presence of a maximum is undoubtedly a safeguard and would be taken to be an assurance that we are not committing into the hands even of judges the determination of the liabilities of the country beyond a certain figure. It would tend, no dou'bt, to still unnecessary apprehensions. I was inclined myself to the view, and I cannot say I am very far from it yet, that on the whole we are better without the maximum. I know there is very considerable opinion the other way. I have no very strong opinion on the question myself, and I shall be glad to hear the views of hon. members. I would presume that if a maximum, were to be fixed the only fair amount to fix would be the minimum amount which the company offered to take during the course of the whole negotiations, and say to the arbitrators: You shall not in any event go beyond that minimum. I know that the representatives of the company would argue : We should not be confined to our minimum, as the maximum may be awarded. It would seem to me, however, that we could not very well fix any maximum beyond the minimum of the company.

As to the cost of the arbitration, the costs incurred by us we will pay, and the costs incurred by the company they will pay. We will pay counsel for the Government, for instance, and I presume we will also pay our own arbitrator. I do not know that any provision has been made for paying the third arbitrator. I have really not thought that out. I cannot say from memory what was done in that regard in the case of the Canadian Northern arbitration, but the Minister of Finance of that time will remember. subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
T quite appreciate the
reasons given by the minister why it would be difficult to fix the maximum now, because before you could arrive at a fair maximum it would be necessary for experts to examine the physical property of the company, its debts, and so on. So we cannot even attempt to fix now what would be a reasonable maximum. Could we not get around the difficulty by providing that as we cannot value the property at this stage, the award of the arbitrators shall not be final and valid until approved and ratified by the Parliament of Canada.
I make the suggestion with the utmost sincerity and not with a view to criticism, and I think my sincerity is evidenced by the fact that I stand with the minister when he says that we cannot now fix the maximum. Now, owing to that very fact that we cannot fix the maximum because of the magnitude of the transaction; owing to the many difficulties which the arbitrators will encounter; in view also of the fact that the real value of the property will be known to Parliament and the people of the country only after the experts have made their report,-in view of all these facts, and many others which I do not mention now, would it not be wise to provide in the Bill that the award should be submitted to Parliament? If this provision were made, I for one, with the feeble means at my disposal, would endeavour to make a thorough study of the whole transaction. I would try to ascertain as nearly as I could the real value of the property in order that I might approach the whole question from a well-informed and intelligent viewpoint. If we are here for anything at all we are here to safeguard the interests of the country, and we should know the exact value of this property, especially when it amounts to hundreds of millions. I would inform myself as well as I could on every

phase of the question, even if it took weeks to do so, and when I came to deal with the award in Parliament, if it were reasonable I would endorse it. I would vote for it because I am not opposed to public ownership, and there are a great many members on this side also who are not opposed to public ownership. Of course, I wish it to be understood that I am speaking only for myself and I commit no one else. So far as I can see the opposition to this measure is not opposition against public ownership. We are discussing the details and we want to have a square deal for the country, and in order that the people's interests may not be in the slightest degree hazarded I earnestly submit to the ministers that it cannot be contended that my suggestion is at all unreasonable that the award should be submitted to Parliament so that every member of the House, even every back bencher on both sides, might have a full opportunity to study it and come to a fair conclusion as to whether it was reasonable or not. I do think that every member should be able to express his opinion on the award, but as the matter now stands we have no real information before us. It is all very well to say that we can ask for what information we require, but so far as I at least am personally concerned, when this matter is concluded in Parliament I shall know very little indeed about it. No one can possibly know anything about the merits of the transaction until he has had an opportunity of studying the evidence of the expert witnesses. I submit this proposal to the consideration of the minister, and. in doing so I should like him to feel that I am actuated by nothing but a sincere desire to protect the interests of the people. I do not make this suggestion in any spirit of criticism, and I should like to have the opinion of the minister in regard to the advisability of submitting the award to Parliament.

speechtext: Very well. I shall now deal with the hon. gentleman's proposal. In the first place, let me correct him. I did not say in my previous remarks that it was impossible to fix a maximum now. I did not say that at all; in fact, I asked for a discussion as to the wisdom of fixing a maximum and suggested that if it were fixed it would seem to me proper that it should be the lowest figure that the shareholders had offered to take. But I do feel that if we are going to fix a maximum the time to do so is now. If we are going to control .ourselves as to what the limit shall be, now is the only time we can do it. Let us. examine the hon. gentleman's suggestion. He says that we should submit this question to arbitration but should not agree to be bound by it. He says it should come back to us afterwards and if we liked it we would take it and if we did not like it it should be rejected. He says further that the shareholders might be given the same privilege. Well, in the first place, why is not that done in the case of all our acquirements of property? By authority of Parliament we have appointed certain men who, in all cases of acquirement of property where the price is not agreed upon-, decide what that price shall be. These men-I refer to the Exchequer Court of Canada-decide questions of that kind year in and year out in connection with, amounts extending to millions. I myself took part on behalf of the country in an arbitration where the claim was $10,000,000, and the question was decided by a .man appointed under the authority of Parliament for that purpose. The Act appointing him-the whole principle of our jurisprudence-does not say that after he decides the question it shall come back to Parliament for Parliament to say whether it will accept the decision or not. But secondly: If it is to come back to Parliament afterwards and we are to decide whether we shall accept the finding or not, and the hon. gentleman is content to allow it to go to the shareholders too, where are we? What progress have we made? What are we going to do in the meantime? Is the Board of Management to take control, and is the process of unification to go on? In short, what is going to happen? It will not have been an arbitration at all, but a fatuous and futile proceeding.

There could not be a more inappropriate comparison. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) .says that we shall know later on what has been decided upon, which information we have not now. He says he will find out. in the meantime, and indicates the means-because he is a lot more logical than many hon. gentlemen who criticise this legislation. He says that he will look over the evidence and see what the expert witnesses say before the court. Then, he says, after we have studied the decision we shall see whether the court is right or not. Does not the absurdity of that suggestion appeal to the hon. gentleman, that if we appoint a judicial tribunal to hear witnesses, to observe their demeanour, and to study the whole problem, making it their business for months, we shall sit as a court of appeal over the evidence they received and determine whether they decided rightly or wrongly? Would that not be really a most absurd position to take? Would not that after all really be a most absurd position to be in? In fact, you cannot argue it. Would we be in a better position to decide as to what was the logical outcome of the evidence of the value of the stock than those who hear the evidence, who are appointed to hear it, whose business it is to do it, and who are trained in that work? Are they not better able to do

that than we who have nothing to do with it, who cannot give the time to it, and who wil' not give the time to it, as every hon. gentleman knows- For these three reasons, first, that it is contrary to the principle of arbitration altogether as proven by the law of this coiuntry as it stands in regard to that subject and the law of every other civilized country; second, because it gets us nowhere and we have no agreement when we are all through, because the arbitration would not accomplish anything and because when we were at the end of it and had incurred all the expense we would be just where we started; and, lastly, because we would *be in no position to review intelligently the judgment which an independent judicial tribunal after hearing the evidence and seeing the witnesses had rendered and whose s'pecial business is to determine rightly and justly.

What I said was that the whole of the arbitration board should not be judges. I believe in looking at the physical assets of this railway. speechtext:
The road should be inspected particularly by a competent man. The rolling stock and all that must be taken into consideration, and these assets should be looked over by somebody. I think a judge is not the best man for that particular work, but he is probably the best man for the head of the court of arbitration. I cast no reflection whatever upon any judges in any of our courts. As to the objections that are raised to fixing a maximum for the award, the minister, before I asked the question, had already stated that we had saved some $800,000 in connection with the Canadian Northern by reason of the fact that we had fixed the award at $10,000,000. The court found that it was worth $10,800,000, but as we had fixed the maximum for the award we saved $800,000; not a large amount surely, but worth while. In this larger matter, where the variation

will be greater, it appears that the fixing of a maximum would not be an unwise proceeding, and to say that the arbitrators will go up to the maximum simply because you fix it is to cast a doubt upon the wisdom of the arbitrators. It is not, an invitation to them to go to the top. It is simply saying you cannot go beyond that unless you come back to Parliament and get our consent. It is not an invitation to them to go up if we fix the award at $20,000,000, or $25,000,000, or $50,000,000. They are supposed to proceed only on the evidence that is before the court, and I claim that it is no invitation to them to go to the exact limit we have fixed. It is rather an intimation that they cannot go beyond that unless they get some further sanction from the people who have to pay the award. It might be argued that if there is a maximum there should be a minimum. I am not sure but that a minimum and a maximum should both be placed. If the shareholders feel that they should have a minimum possibly it might be a matter for consideration. In the case of the Canadian Northern, the fixing of a maximum worked out slightly to our advantage.
I commend these further considerations to the attention of the minister. I am not taking strong ground upon them, and I do not wish to obstruct the clause, but I think the crux of the whole situation, the valuation which is to be found, is largely bound up in this clause. The outcome will depend largely on the kind of arbitrators we will get. It is important that the interests of the country shall be safeguarded in every possible way, as there can be no doubt that a further blow will be struck at public ownership if we start off by paying far too high a price for the intrinsic assets of the Grand Trunk. I do not wish to cast any imputation upon the Board of Arbitration, but we are doing something that, is going to cost money and the interest of the country ought to be protected in every possible way. I only make these suggestions to the minister-lie was the physical assets of the Grand Trunk. I spoke-in the hope that he will give them his earnest consideration. If there is nothing in them I feel that I have at least discharged a duty which I felt it incumbent upon me to discharge in pointing out what I believe are necessary safeguards, and in the endeavour to ensure that this arbitration board, when appointed, will be the best that can be got for the work that it is intended to do.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I think the minister dismissed rather too summarily

the suggestion made by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) as to the possible application of the principle of ihe Industrial Disputes Act to this measure. The Industrial Disputes Act applies to disputes between railway companies and their employees. As hon. members know, under that Act each of the parties has the right to name a member of the board, the two agree upon a third and when the/ give their award it is open to the public, and public opinion may express itself in reference to it. The theory underlying the Act is that public opinion in the last analysis will determine what is right and that will be the instrument whereby right will be enforced. Consequently the Act proceeds on the theory that if the award is a fair one it will be backed up by public opinion and the parties will in the long run accept it. On the other hand the Act takes it for granted that if the award is unfair to either party, or to both, before it is made binding upon them each shall have the opportunity of directing public attention to. the element of unfairness in it.
The situation here is almost identical. The Government has asked that a board of arbitrators shall pass upon some uncertain and unknown quantity because the value of the stock as it exist is unknown by either of the parties. If the arbitrators give an award which is justified by the evidence before them and' which seems reasonable, such award will receive the support of public opinion and as such it will certainly bind the two parties. The two parties will accept it with good will because it will be obviously an award which has public opinion back of it. As I understand the remarks of my hon. friend from Nelson, that is what he feels should be done in this case. He believes that the award o.f the arbitrators should be made public and that each of the parties should have an opportunity of saying whether or not they think the award fair under all the circumstances. If it is not fair they should have an opportunity of pointing out wherein the unfairness consists.
If we were proceeding in this kind of transaction for the first time we might perhaps be prepared to accept all that has been said about the absence of any necessity for fear as to the consequences of a measure of this kind. But I submit that if we study this transaction it will be found to be very much on all fours with that which took place some time ago when the Government acquired the properties of
the Canadian Northern. At that time there was a stock which was supposed to be practically of no value. It was referred to a board of arbitrators to put a valuation upon it and the country paid in Consequence, without any opportunity of accepting or rejecting the award, something like $10,009,000. Well, when the country has been stung once for a sum amounting to $10,000,000, through procedure of this kind, I think we are justified in asking the Government whether it is not wise to protect the country against being stung a second time-not for $10,000,000, perhaps, but for many times $10,000,000; -we have no idea at the moment what the amount will be.

I simply say to my hon. friend, as I have already remarked, that I will not ask him to accept my word; I will give him the view of one whose name, I believe, is more honoured than the name of any other man who has ever sat in the halls of this Parliament-I mean the late Sir Wilfrid I.aurier. The country will agree with the estimate which I have placed on Sir Wilfrid Laurier's character, and I will now give the hon. gentleman Sir Wilfrid's opinion in reference to the transaction to which he has referred. In the last public address which Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave to the people of Canada, he spoke thus of the acquisition of the Canadian Northern railway:
One feature of the Act of last session is that the Government -becomes the owner of the stock of the company, of the nominal value

of sixty million dollars. There never wae a dollar paid on that stock. The experts employed by the Government to appraise the value of the whole enterprise, men of acknowledged ability and experience, themselves have reported that the stock of the company has no value whatever.
Yet the Government have taken authority to appoint a board of arbitrators to give a value to that property, which their experts have declared absolutely without value.
The Opposition asked that the report of the arbitrators, whatever it might be, should be laid before Parliament for approval. Though this motion was rejected, it is the right of the people to declare that the case should not have been finally closed by the action of a moribund Parliament, but that the whole matter should be reported to, and adjudicated upon, by the new Parliament.
I would say to the minister that the only particular, it seems to me, in which what the Government is proposing at the present time in this measure differs from what I have already read in regard to the Canadian Northern railway transaction is, that instead of regard for the people's rights being precluded by the action of a moribund Parliament it is being precluded at this time by the action of a government which has already lost the confidence of the country- if public opinion as it is evidenced from every side is any indication at all-The rights of the people are being absolutely usurped at the instance of a ministry which has no justification in proceeding with a transaction of these proportions without giving opportunity for some expression by the people of Canada upon it. Now I want to make clear that this transaction is on all fours with the Canadian Northern, because I think the country understands pretty well what the latter transaction'amounted to. Speaking of the Canadian Northern transaction the quotation which I have just read has the following:
The experts employed by the Government to appraise the value of ' the whole enterprise,
. men of acknowledged ability and experience, themselves have reported that the stock of the company has no value whatever.
Here is an exact parallel. We have before us the report of the Drayton-Acwortb Commission, and the minister will hardly say that the members of that commission were not men of acknowledged ability and experience. Yet what does the Drayton-Acworth report say in reference to the value of this stock? At page 65 of the report this statement is to be found:
Even if the Government were to relieve them entirely,-
-that is the Grand Trunkas suggested by their president, of their unfortunate Grand Trunk Pacific venture-and

as we have already said, we cannot think that this request can be reasonably justified-it is evident that the Grand Trunk Company is not, and will not be for some time to come, in a position entitling it to pay out any money at all in dividends. We regard the entire share capital of the company as being intrinsically of but small value at the present time. On the basis of present value of maintainable income the fair compensation would be very small.
So that, in regard to this transaction, we have gentlemen of experience and ability informing Parliament that even if the Government were to relieve the Grand Trunk entirely of the Grand Trunk Pacific-which they say it should not do, but which the Government is doing by this measure-the entire share capital of the company is intrinsically but of small value. The parallel is therefore entirely an exact one with the case that I have already mentioned. Now, in what particular is there a further parallel? The further parallel is that the Opposition is asking the Government to do exactly what it .asked should be done in the case of the Canadian Northern transaction, with the view of avoiding the situation I have described. The Opposition asked that the report of the arbitrators, whatever it might be, should be laid before Parliament for approval. Had the Government, in the matter of the Canadian Northern deal, submitted the award of the arbitrators to Parliament for approval, then it would have been for Parliament to say whether this country should have given out $10,060,000 for stock in regard to which not a single dollar of value had been put in. So we on this side contend that inasmuch as we have before us, and the country has before it a transaction of the kind which I have just made reference to, there is the strongest reason why its appeal to the ministry to have the award of the Board of Arbitrators placed before Parliament should be heeded at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The essence ol this transaction is the amount of money the people of Canada will have to pay as a consequence of this arbitration.^ My hon. friend raises the question of judicial decisions to make it appear that we are in some way attacking the judiciary. As I pointed out to him yesterday, there is one obvious limitation to the legal mind; it is apt to run along legal lines so exclusively that it sometimes cannot appreciate just how the public, who are not wholly familiar with legal methods and legal technicalities, will view certain questions. This is a question that affects the taxpayers of this country, and is going to affect them for the next thirty years and more. It is a transaction that is going to impose enormous liabilities on this country at a time when, of all times, the country is least able to shoulder them. What we are suggesting is that before this terrific liability, unknown at the present time, and which may amount to anything, is put upon the shoulders of his country, bound and manacled there so that it cannot be removed for a generation, there should be some opportunity given to public opinion to express itself throughout the country and through its representatives in this House. I must thank the minister for making clear the distinction between us in our estimates of public opinion. My Liberalism leads me to believe that public opinion has a right to have its voice heard and its influence felt in this Parliament before this transaction is consummated. The minister's view is that public opinion should be ignored altogether. That we should proceed only alone the lines that he as a lawyer is prepared to recommend to this House is in accord, I think, with the oldest form of Toryism known to the world.

speechtext: The Government's offer was $2,500,000 [DOT] for the first three years, $3,000,000 for the next five years, and $3,600,000 annually there after for the balance of 999 years. I could not say just what that would amount to if distributed over the whole 999 years in equal annual amounts, although I did hear an actuarial calculation of it, and I think it was about $3,330,000 odd per annum; that is, the Government's offer was equivalent to saying they would pay $3,330,000 odd every year of the 999 years. The Government is going to pay $2,500,000 on the guaranteed stock; that would leave 830,000 odd dollars per year. So if the arbitrators' award is on that basis it will about equal our offer. The Government, of course, contends that nothing should be paid beyond $2,500,000, and that will be our contention before the board of arbitration. I was not in the House
during the past two days when the question came up as to how this stock was to be

valued, but I understand there was some discussion about fixing a day or date from which the arbitrators would proceed. That would indicate that the arbitrators will take into consideration the value of the stocks on the London market from time to time.
If that be so, I submit that it is not going to get us anywhere. For this reason the stocks on the London stock exchange, not only of the Grand Trunk but other stocks more or less speculative, are handled by manipulators and speculators, and it very rarely represents the actual value of the physical assets of the various companies. As I understand it, some of these stocks, particularly the guaranteed stock, for which we are going to guarantee four per cent, a few years ago dropped to about twenty cents in the dollar. Time and again this guaranteed stock passed its dividend.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No. The guaranteed stock did not time and again pass dividends at all. It just passed two years.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The junior securities had become only gambling counters on the stock exchange.
Where did the cause lie? There was not one; there were several. The first was in capitalization. The line had been hopelessly over-capitalized to begin with, and the new acquisitions doubled fixed charges, while net receipts increased only ten per cent; feeders had proved suckers.
This is an extract from chapter 11 on the expansion of the Grand Trunk in a book by Professor Skelton, who made an exhaustive study of ,the subject.
If we are to arrive at the proper value of these stocks it must be done by taking the physical assets and liabilities and valuing them in that way. In no other way can we arrive at any proper valuation of the stock. If we fall back upon the values of the London stock exchange we are in the hands of stock gamblers and thimble-riggers.

Before the clause carries I desire to make a statement to the committee with regard thereto. I am glad to say, and I hope it will meet with the approval of the committee, that instead of leaving to any chance at all the appointment of the third arbitrator, which appointment, as hon. members know, is one of the most vital factors in the whole solution of the problem, the consent of Mr. Justice Cassels of the Exchequer Court has been obtained to act as third arbitrator. Sub-
[The Chairman.]
ject to the approval of Parliament in this regard, as in all others, we are prepared to insert a provision in the. clause that Chief Justice Cassels of the Exchequer Court shall be the third arbitrator.

speechtext:
No, shall be the third
arbitrator himself. I think it is peculiarly desirable that he should be selected for the reason that he is the head of the court that determine all values as between the country and individual citizens and his experience extending over many years, as well as his reputation for the highest integrity and ability, peculiarly fits him to be the custodian of the rights of all in this regard. I therefore propose to offer an amendment to the effect that the third arbitrator be Sir Walter Cassels, judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada and that in the event of the death or other inability of the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court to act the two arbitrators so appointed shall select a third. I cannot give the exact wording of the amendment because the wording as submitted to me does not adjust itself to the wording of the clause, but I shall read what will be made to fit into the clause and submit the amendment later:
The board of arbitrators shall consist of three members, one to ;be appointed by the Government, one by the Grand Trunk and the third shall be Sir Walter Cassels, Judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada. Should Sir Walter Cassels be unable to act the said parties shall select a third arbitrator who shall be either a judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada or one of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister has given the history of the acquisition by the Government of property. I remember that the acquisition of rights of way of railways was entirely in the hands of a committee. In 1886, 1887 or 1888 the Intercolonial was extended through the island of Cape Breton. I was then a law student in Sydney and I remember meeting this committee which used to go all over Canada appraising rights of way. This was a committee appointed by the Government, but in time, as the matter wms one of importance, jurisdiction was taken from that committee and vested in the Exchequer Court. If an agreement cannot be reached between the Department

oi Railways and Canals and the owner of land, the Exchequer Court has jurisdiction as the court of first resort. There is no fault to be found with that procedure. I am not so strong on the point now since we have been told that the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court is to have a prominent part in this arbitration, but I was going to suggest to the Government the feasibility of leaving this matter entirely to the Exchequer Court.
The Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court is to be the third man in this arbitration and everybody will admit that the third man is the important person in the arbitration. An arbitration court is after all a very poor court. Both sides start out with a representative in the court, each determined to uphold the case of his client. The Grand Trunk selects a man who will stand for it; we select a man we think will stand for us. This man is biased in our favour, and the other man is biased in favour of the Grand Trunk. The whole business seems to hinge on the impartiality and ability of the third man. No one will say that a court that must reach its decision by a compromise is the best kind of a court. If the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court -is to be the third man, if he is to be the chief motive power, if he is to take the heavy oar in reaching a conclusion, why not leave the matter to the Exchequer Court entirely and do not embarrass the court with two other men who will be pulling in opposite directions, and each doing his utmost to find a way of getting a decision in favour of his own interest? We bought the Quebec and Saguenay and another railway in the province of Quebec not very long ago. We passed an Act conferring jurisdiction on the Exchequer Court to make a valuation of these properties. I think the way in which the judge of the Exchequer Court handled that case was highly satisfactory. It may not have been satisfactory to everybody, but the business way in which it was dealt with by the judge commends that method of procedure to me. We all recognize the ability and integrity of the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court. He is a man who is particularly well fitted to deal with questions of this kind. I can see no good reason for not leaving this whole question to the Exchequer Court. It is the only court we have in Canada to deal with a matter of this kind. It has ample scope to call witnesses from all parts of the country. It can sit anywhere in Canada and then finally give its decision.
96 J
I do not see, Mr. Chairman, why, when we have such machinery expressly for the purpose of dealing with questions of this kind, we should be travelling outside and worrying ourselves about arbitration. This is an absolutely capable court of the highest possible reputation, and our friends in England, or any other part of the world, who have to deal with the value of these stocks should be satisfied to leave Judge Cassels try the case and file his decision. These are reasons which appeal to me. When we have once established the principle I do not see that there is very much difference in dealing with a small railroad as compared with a big one. The railroad in Quebec is not so very small and if we found this procedure most satisfactory in ascertaining its value, I do not see why we would not apply the same machinery and the same principle to a bigger road. If there is any good reason why we should not do so, I think the House and the country are entitled to know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman in suggesting that we should have submitted this matter purely and simply to the judge of the Exchequer Court, pointed out that as he looked on this Arbitration Board it would he composed of one man urging the interests of the Grand Trunk, a second man urging the interests of the Government, and that the third arbitrator v ould be the important man and the deciding factor. If that view be correct we are substantially leaving this matter to the determination of the judge of the Exchequer Court and getting the same practical result that we would get, if that point of view be correct, as we would by submitting it to the judge of the Exchequer Court alone. On the other hand, I think there is this to be taken into consideration: Even though we suppose the two other arbitrators who would be associated with the judge may each, on his own side, approach the subject with a greater disposition to see greater strength on the part of the claims of those who have selected him, they will bring to that tribunal- at all events the providing for it makes possible that there should be brought to that tribunal-the aid and the assistance of experts with regard to these matters, and who may be of valuable assistance to the judge of the Exchequer Court in dealing with these questions. It is not an uncommon thing in courts-particularly where they are called upon to deal with matters of this kind, where the possession of great technical knowledge may be of considerable value- to call in skilled persons, described as as-

sessors. whose assistance is found to be valuable in practice. Now there is a third matter I would like to point out as distinguishing this case from cases where we proceed to expropriate property in connection with railways, or to acquire a railway by a process of expropriation. It is to be borne in mind that here we are proceeding to acquire the s-tdck of this company by an agreement with those interested, and we are not therefore in a position to impose upon them a particular Court; their views as to the composition of the board that should determine the difference that exists as to the value of the property to be acquired must be taken into consideration. So long as we are endeavouring to reach an agreement there would perhaps be something arbitrary in our undertaking to impose upon the other party to the agreement the obligation of submitting this difference between us to a particular court. I point out again that we are not proceeding by expropriation; we are endeavouring to provide a tribunal which will be accepted by both of the parties to the proposed agreement. Apart from that consideration-, I do think there are some possible advantages, as I have already -pointed out, by an association with the Exchequer Court judge of the men that it is possible at all events will be designated; and ultimately, in actual practical results, we get, as the hon. gentleman himself has pointed out, the determination of this question by the Judge of the Exchequer court.
-Mr. FIELDING: Would not the Judge of the Exchequer Court be in a better position to obtain that technical knowledge by calling in technical advisers-assessors, as they are sometimes called in other cases

rather than take the chance of getting technical men under this method? For example, the Government of Canada will appoint an arbitrator and there is nothing which says he must he a technical man. The Grand Trunk may appoint an -arbitrator, and there is nothing which says he must be a technical -man. In -both cases they are appointed as arbitrators, although it may or may not be thought that technical men are the best. If therefore technical knowledge is required it would strike me that the Judge of the Exchequer Court could better get it by calling in the aid of assessors than by the method proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I would point out the fact that if it- should turn out that neither of the men who are to be associated with the judge have that requisite technical

knowledge, there is nothing to preclude the arbitrators from taking the necessary means to otherwise acquire that technical information.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I might s-ay to the Minister of Justice that we have the worldwide experience of trial courts consisting of one judge. If in its wisdom and experience Parliament, either in this country or elsewhere, had found that two or three judges would constitute a better trial court than one jud-ge, no doubt long ago we would- have had more than one judge constituted as a trial court. My own absolute belief is that one man tries a case better than two or three. For that reason I am in favour of the judge of the Exchequer Court sitting to try this case -alone, rather than having two men associated with him, one pulling against the other. Of course, if there are three men sitting down in a court-with a view to getting at the truth, that may be an advantage; but I submit- to the Minister of Justice that his experience of many years on the Supreme Court Bench would teach him that he would want to have absolutely his own free mind, and his own judgment, in trying this case, and not be interfered with by the opinion of somebody else. He will reach his own conclusions and follow his own decisions; but he would not like to be pulled and hauled by one on each side of him who was entirely of a different view and trying to reach a different conclusion. That is not the kind of men I would like to have sitting on the Bench with me, but that is the position in which we are going to put Mr. Justice Cassels, who is accustomed to trying cases alone, and to filing his own decisions without any interference. Here we place him as a buffer between two of the ablest men that perhaps can be got in this country, one of whom is pulling him one way and the other pulling him another way. I d-o not think we can get the best results from Judge Cassels under -conditions of that kind. I would like to see him with a free hand to deal with this matter, and I would like there to be an appeal from his decision to a higher court, just as in the case of any other decision that he -might make. Speaking for myself, I would prefer to leave this very big question in -that form rather than leave it to a conflict between two men, with Judge Cassels doing the best he can to keep them straight.

speechtext: Why does not the Government leave the management of the road to the company until the stock is acquired?
