subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I still contend that as this clause stands it gives the right of ratification to the shareholders and does not permit an equal right to Parliament. When we were asking why it was that this Bill was being rushed it was stated that it was desirable to have the agreement drawn as soon as possible. There will be an opportunity to draw the agreement, but according to this section the agreement will not have any value one way or the other until a special general meeting of the stockholders has been duly called for the purpose of considering it. By the time the agreement is drawn and the special meeting of stockholders has passed upon it another couple of months shall have gone by and Parliament will be again in session. There could be no delay to either of the parties by permitting Parliament when it reassembles to have the same opportunity of passing on the agreement as the shareholders of the Grand Trunk will have. I would urge again on the Government, on
behalf of the people, that the people's representatives be accorded the same privileges and rights as will be given to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Whom will the Committee of Management be ansrwerable to? The Minister of Railways a few nights ago made this statement:
Any agent who does not act on that principle will not, while I am Minister of Railways, be on the job very long.
The minister told us a year ago that the Government were not interfering with the management of the Canadian National railway, but on October 23, on page 1372-3 unrevised Hansard, he said that an^ agent who disobeyed his orders while he was Minister of Railways would " not he on the job very long." I would ask what is the position these commissioners will occupy. Will they be directly under the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The management will be under the direction of the Grand Trunk Railway system.
, Mr. CAHILL: So that the two directors will have nothing to do hut draw the Cana- ' dian people's money. They will not be responsible to any one?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Committee of Management is just exactly as set out in the Bill. We have representation on the committee, and the Grand Trunk have representation on it equally. One commissioner is chosen by the four, and those five have the management of the Grand Trunk. Our representatives will be responsible to us for what they do, and their representatives will be responsible to them. It is an independent joint system of management. It was a plan thought out in order to cover the period between the making of the agreement and the final determination of the arbitration. It is a sort of joint management in the meantime in order that the owners of the propertyjnay not give it up until at least the arbitration award is made, and in order, on the other hand, that the advantage toward which we are all striving, namely, the unification of the roads, may be secured at once.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Two will be appointed
by the Government who will be answerable to the Government, and two will be appointed by the Grand Trunk answerable to the Grand Trunk. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Answerable in the sense that it is their duty to see from cur standpoint that the road is properly run. I do not suppose that they will be making daily

reports to us or anything of that sort. They are a joint independent management of the system.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
To whom will the fifth
commissioner be answerable?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: He will be answerable, I presume, first to his own conscience, and then to both the country and the company.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If he has not more conscience than is displayed by some ministers it will be unfortunate for the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Order. I must ask the hon. member to withdraw that remark; it certainly is unparliamentary.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I bow to your decision,
Mr. Chairman.. Will the commissioners be responsible to the Minister of Railways- that is, the commissioners the Government appoint?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I have stated their responsibility.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister has . told us that this is to be a joint system of management, two men to be appointed by the Grand Trunk and two by the Government. Assuming that there is a loss in running the road for the first two or three months during'which they are acting will the Government, or will the company, find the money to make up the deficit?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: As I understand the point which my hon. friend raises it is this: Who bears the loss, and who receives the gains, if any, during the currency of the committee's management? The Grand Trunk stockholders are the owners of the stock until the determination of the award.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is, when the stock is delivered to the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Up to that the loss will be borne by the railway company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think that is quite correct. Presuming that the valuation of the stock is fixed as of October 1, 1919, we would, immediately after the determination of the arbitration, issue our stock in payment for their stock and we would become the stockholders. The Grand Trunk is liable for all the obligations of the road then just as it is now. We are the owners of the stock of the Grand Trunk and we take the company, of course, subject to,the obligations. We do not stand the loss except in so far as our stock may be affected

in value by it. We become the owners of the stock at that time, and of course the stock is affected in value by the liabilities of the company on the one hand and by the value of the assets of the company on the other. If the assets are increased by the management that reflects itself in an increase in the stock; if the liabilities are increased, that has a deteriorating effect on the value of the stock. It is the Grand Trunk Company which then as now stands the loss; it is the Grand Trunk Company which then, as now, receives the gain if there should be any.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That does not seem to be quite clear. Who pays the money? Suppose we are operating the road in the name of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, in reality it is the Government of Canada. In reality the Grand Trunk is merely a sign, a name. If there is money made it belongs to the Government; if there is money lost it is lost to the Government, If we lose money in the interim while the road is under this management, if it is found that $100,000 or $500,000 is necessary to keep the machinery going, that money has to come out of some part of the revenues of Canada. It does not come out of any pocket of the company. It has no money at all but we .stand behind it and must furnish the money. Therefore it does not do any good to talk about this stock. Once we get the stock and put it in the safe it is a mere nominal thing; the question of what it is worth 'to the people does not cut any ice. They do not care a button about it; they only take it as a means of getting this property. Now that they have the property, they can run it in the name of the Minister oif Railways or in the name of the Grand Trunk, if they like. It is identically the *same property and if it makes a loss it is in the same position as the Intercolonial. What was asked of the minister was: Supposing that at the end of one, ot five months under the management of this commission of five there is a shortage of $1,000 or $10,000, who will make it good? My contention is that if the earnings of the road are not enough to meet the liabilities we must make up the shortage. If that is not so I would like to have an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We are just in the same relation to the company as are the stockholders of any other company. The company has to pay it. We may run the company but the company is the one that suffers.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We .are the company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, we are the stockholders. That is a different thing altogether. Of course, we are gainers by the success of the company and we are losers by the non success of the company simply because we are stockholders in the company. It is better for the company that there should be this joint management in order that the two systems may be run .as one as .soon as possible because that is the way to get the best results from the two systems. That being the position, it is better for the company, and consequently it is better for us as stockholders of the company, that that should take place.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is not very clear to my mind and I cannot see it in the same way as the minister does. When do we become the owners of this .stock; when do we become the proprietors of the Grand .Trunk system? Is it not at the date of the delivery of the stock that we become the owners?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Well, then, it is apparent that any loss prior to that should not be borne by the Government; it should be borne by the company. They must deliver us the property before we begin to pay for the losses. The board of arbitrators should fix the date on which the property can be delivered to the .Government, and prior to that time any loss should fall upon the company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I say it falls on the company.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The shareholders should have the amount of the loss deducted from the .price of their stock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The shareholders "have not the management of the property during that loss. This is a sort of joint method of meeting the opposing views of the committee in this regard. It is true we do not become the legal owners of the stpck until the transfer to us takes place subsequent to the award, but I think I am using legal language strictly correctly when. I say that we become the equitable owners immediately the agreement is acted on.. We are bound to be the owners of the company then. We await the legal title pending the award but we are virtually the owners immediately the agreement takes effect; we abide legal possession until the stock is handed over. They get their stock valued as of a certain date, but immediately the agreement is
signed we become the virtual owners of the property and consequently the value of our stock will be, affected by the success or failure of the company.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Grand Trunk should not appoint these managers at all if we are to become the equitable owners at that time. If the committee of management is appointed, why should the Grand Trunk have anything to do with the appointment? They cease to be the owners, we become the. equitable owners, and yet they have the right to appoint two of the members upon the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I admit there is something to (be said for that viewpoint. It appealed to me before this, but there is a lot to be said the other way and this is the method that has been devised for taking care of the difficulty. The Grand Trunk Company say: " It is true you are going to be the owners; as soon as the agreement is signed on a fixed date you will be the owners; but you should not have the right to take full possession, come in and man our property "

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: ''Even if you are the owners"?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No-"until, at all
events, we know what- we are going to get for it." Now, in the case of the Canadian Northern something similar was done by the Government, although I think we went more fully into possession there than we do here. "Under that arrangement, we appointed directors on the board, who operated with the other directors pending the final award. Now the plan adopted here to meet the opposing views was that a general committee of management should operate in the meantime leaving the Grand Trunk organization there so that they could not say they were dispossessed of the property-thrown out bag and baggage, as they might if we took possession of the whole thing and had all the officers under our hands, making it unreasonably difficult for them to get the evidence that was necessary. There was considerable to be said for their point of view and there is considerable to be said the other way. All I can add is, this is what was deemed a fair arrangement between the two.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Can the minister give any estimate as to the time when these stocks will be transferred?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I think the Bill, or the letter says, nine months. I would not like to say they can be transferred in that time,

tut I earnestly hope that they can. The transfer of the stock is not so vital a matter because if it is not .transferred immediately after the award is made the Governor in Council has full power to declare it the property of the Crown 'and pay for it according to the award.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The committee is to be discharged on the date when the preferred and common stock is transferred?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: "Or vested," it says.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister thinks that will be nine months?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is the time within which it has to be done. I would like to see it done sooner. If I were called upon to give my estimate I would not say it would take that time.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is there any provisions for the appointment of a fifth member of the committee in the event of a dispute taking place between the others?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is no provision for that. We did not think it was probable that four business men could not agree on a fifth man.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is, of course, a very large staff of managers in connection with the various companies now. Are they to be superseded by this committee of management, or will the present management be subordinate to the committee, and by what arrangement is that brought about?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: By virtue of the Bill the present management is Subordinated to the committee of management, not displaced, but subordinated to it.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the minister be kind enough to tell me if the majority of the holders of the stock referred to in this particular clause mean a majority in value or in number of stockholders?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: A majority in voting power.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The clause does not say so, and therefore it is probably better to make its meaning clearer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Possibly it would.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Would the minister com-sent to an amendment to that effect?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The opinion expressed from a legal standpoint is that that is what it means now. I would certainly be ready to accept an amendment if there was any 
doubt at all about it, but I understand that to be the legal effect now.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, in discussing not only this clause, but the preceding clauses, used the word " agreement." I am at times in doubt as to what agreement is meant. For instance, there is an agreement mentioned in section 2 .and that is the one by which the Government is given the power to acquire the entire capital, and so on. In the first line of section 7 the phrase used is " said agreement." I assume that refers to the submission to arbitration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That is a defined term, defined: in section 2, which says:
Subject to the provisions of this Act, His Majesty the King, represented by the Minister of Railways and Canals of Canada, acting under the authority of the Governor in Council, (hereinafter called " the Government '') may enter into an agreement (hereinafter called the " said agreement ") with the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
It is a defined term.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Then does the phrase in this section mean the agreement referred to in section 2?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: And it is the submission to arbitration?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The agreement referred to in the section is the submission to arbitration.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Not having the language of the amendment that was made to section 6 before me, T do not know whether the words " said agreement '' in line 9 have disappeared as a result of that amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They have disappeared?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
There is another observation called for with reference to that. In paragraph (a) of section 7 the language used is as follows:
A committee of management shall be formed consisting of five persons, two to be appointed by the Grand Trunk, two by the Government, and the fifth by the four so appointed, to insure the operation of the Grand Trunk system (in so far as it is possible so to do) in harmony with the Canadian National Railways, the two systems being treated in the public interest as nearly as possible as one system'.
Now in the blue-book containing the correspondence and other data relating to this transaction which was brought down, it is shown that there are 1,665 miles owned, controlled or leased by the Grand Trunk

system in the United States. My hon. friend for Shelburne and Queens (Mr Fielding) in the earlier stages of the discussion-perhaps it was on the second reading -asked the Minister of the Interior, or some other member of the Government, if any inquiry had been made as to whether or not there was any objection on the part of the United States Government to the operation by the Canadian Government of a railway system in United States territory. My recollection is that the answer was that no inquiry had been made and no objection was known-in other words, the Government had not any information on the subject. It occurred to me at the time as a very important matter, and I have taken the trouble to make inquiry at Washington. The subject, I may say, is brought up again by the concluding words of the clause which I have just read. Now, my information from official circles in Washington is that if the United States Government take over the operation of the railroads in that country the Canadian Government will have to obtain permission to operate that portion of the Grand Trunk railway within United States territory. On the other hand, if the United States Government do not take over the roads in the United States, there will in any event, be a new system inaugurated there called the " zoning ' system whereby certain groups of railroads will be restricted to operation within certain defined zones having some large centre of population as the pivotal point within the zone, and subject to other regulations. From that point of view the operation of that portion of the Grand Trunk railway within the territory of the United States will be subject to some regulation of the United States Government or of the controlling railway authority in that country. From either point of view, I submit, this Government should be in possession of information and such information as they may have the committee is entitled to receive. In any case, I bring the matter to the attention of the Government now so that if there is any information available they might give it now and if not we ought to receive it before the Bill- is put through its last stages.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Assuming that the information which the hon. gentleman gives is right-and I see nothing in it to make it probable that it is wrong-no difficulty whatever is presented. If the United States continue operation of their roads, then it will deal with roads belonging to companies the stock of which is owned by the
Canadian Government just in the same way as they will deal with roads belonging to companies the stock of which is owned by somebody else. We expect that; we would never ask for anything beyond that. We expect to be treated the same as other people, at all events in relation to lines in American territory. Now, suppose the other alternative be adopted by the United States, of placing their roads under some new system on the zone principle; Then, too, all that we would expect would be the same treatment of companies owned by the Grand Trunk, whose stock we own, as of any other company in the United States. That is all we expect; that they will do with it just as they would have done if Sir Alfred Smithers and his associates and all the hundred thousand shareholders had remained owners of the Grand Trunk stock. In a word, there is no reason to apprehend any different treatment of the Grand Trunk or of any subsidiary company owned or leased by it after the Government becomes the owner of the stock of the parent company than was the case before. Consequently, there is no reason to apprehend any adverse attitude on the part of the United States authorities.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If there is a probability that it would have an effect on the values, then that should certainly be taken into account by the board.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) raised a point about the meaning of "majority of the holders of the stocks". The rule of construction in

such cases as this is, that the natural meaning attaching to the language is to be accepted unless there is a clear legal understanding to the contrary, and the natural understanding of this language would be that it meant a majority of heads, so to speak, not a majority in value. Take the simple example of five men owning stock, one owning ten shares and the other four one share each. If the construction which the minister puts upon
9 p.m, this is correct,-and perhaps it is-the one man who has ten shares would control the other four, because they hold a total of only four shares as against the one man's ten. But unless we were forced to do so we would scarcely conclude that the one man was a majority of these stockholders. I have always found a distinction made by writers on companies between majority in numbers and majority in value.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I will accept an amendment to cover the point raised by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Parent); I suggest that the words: "in voting power" be inserted after the word "majority" in the second line of section 7. I suggest these words instead of the words "in value," because the shareholders do not vote according to value. My information is that the section as at present worded has legal effect, although I do not remember any decision on the point. However, there will be no doubt about it if the words "in voting power" are put in.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I notice that the four per cent guaranteed stock has a voting power of' 400,000 and the debenture stocks, which are also guaranteed by the Dominion Government under this arrangement, a voting power of 1,161,952, or a total of 1,561,952, representing more than half the total voting power of the combined shares, debenture, preference and common. The four per cent guaranteed stocks are being enhanced in value and become a paying stock instead of a stock which is not paying; and the debenture stocks, two of them at four per cent, are also enhanced in value by the guarantee of the Dominion Government. It is quite conceivable that the holders of these stocks and debentures would sanction this arrangement, and that the owners of the shares-really the minority of the shares-that are to be arbitrated would oppose the arbitration. Would the Government consider it advisable to go on with the arrangement if a majority of the

owners of the shares which are to be arbitrated opposed the arbitration?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, the Government would feel it its duty to do so if the Grand Trunk shareholders, with the voting -power to which each shareholder is legally entitled and always has been, carry the agreement. I have not figured out how this voting power stands. But they have among themselves agreed on this voting strength; that i= their business; it is really not ours.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: When did they agree upon this voting strength with respect to the guaranteed stock?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: When they subscribed the money. That is the condition on which they subscribe it and take their shares. Consequently we can get their verdict only as they can legally give it. If the arrangement is net fair, it is not for us to make it fair.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Do the Government consider that they would be justified in going on if a certain set of stocks were taken care of and made virtually bonds as the minister states they will be? This $60,000,000 worth of stocks is virtually made into bonds by this transaction, and the other bonds are enhanced in value. Certain sets of these securities are selected and enhanced in value, perhaps to the detriment of the others. Would we not possibly be buying a lawsuit if we undertake the thing on that basis?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The answer I gave fully covers the point. I presume those who put the bulk of the money in and who have the first claims would not care to put themselves into the power of the last mortgagees. If the last mortgagees are to have control, they might simply hold on and allow the first men to fall with them. Taking all those things into account, they have arranged this distribution of their voting strength, and by the exercise of their voting strength so distributed they can legally bind themselves. That is all their concern. When they legally bind themselves, then we accept their decision so expressed.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Did I understand the
minister to say in answer to the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) that the Government intended to proceed irrespective of what vote the stockholders might give at the meeting called to consider this agreement?

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) gave as a reason for appointing this committee that there was a necessity of immediate exchange of traffic at certain points. The .minister mentioned an exchange of traffic at North Bay. Is there any connection now between the main system of the Grand Trunk and North Bay, owned and controlled by the Grand Trunk? If not, what is the connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Grand Trunk exchanges traffic at North Bay with our present Canadian Northern system.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: How do we get to North Bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The main line of the Grand Trunk runs from Toronto to North Bay, and. we can also get to North Bay via the Canada Atlantic. -

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am told that in getting traffic to the main line of the Transcontinental from the Grand Trunk we have to make use of the Ontario Government-owned railway, the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario. Is that a fact? Have we any traffic arrangement with the Government of Ontario in connection with that road?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Grand Trunk system have some kind of running rights. If they run a train over that road, they pay a certain mileage rate for so doing. That is the only way in which the Grand Trunk can get to the Transcontinental at present. When we take over the Grand Trunk and it becomes part of the Transcontinental, at North Bay we would connect with the Canadian Northern.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: As regards routing of freight, when we own the road, we would have no purpose, would we, in changing any of the arrangements existing under the present status of the Grand Trunk-that is .in connection with all the traffic that they are carrying now to the best advantage of the road as they think?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Yes we would, for this reason. The Grand Trunk to-day when it gets to North Bay may hand its freight over to the Canadian Pacific, or it may want to get a longer haul and may send it via Sarnia and from there over some line of steamers to Port Arthur and there hand it to the Canadian Pacific to carry it through to Calgary or Edmonton or the coast. We have no control over that at present. For instance, the hon. member may want to ship a carload of merchandise from Montreal to Vancouver., The Grand Trunk Railway Company might say: We will take that as far as we can on our system, up to Sarnia; then we will ship it by a line of steamers to Port Arthur, and from Port Arthur by rail via the Canadian Pacific to Vancouver. Or they might ship it to Owen Sound or Midland and let the Canadian Pacific steamers take it from there to Port Arthur and from Port Arthur by rail to Vancouver. We lose all that haul under present conditions. If we have control of the Grand Trunk, we have the advantage, of which I was speaking a few minutes ago, of having all Ontario and Quebec traffic now controlled by the Grand Trunk being transferred to the Canadian National railway. We would be in this position, that if we wanted to send freight, say, to Vancouver, we could route it to North Bay and then over the Canadian Northern system right through to Vancouver. If we wanted to send it lake and rail, we could send it up to Goderich, hand it over there to the line of steamers that now plies on the lakes in connection with the Canadian Northern, and in that way the Canadian Northern would get the advantage of that additional freight of which they do not get one pound now. Then when the freight reached Port Arthur, it would go over the 'Canadian Northern system right through to Vancouver. The result would be that we would get all that long haul, and an immense quantity of freight that we do not receive now at all. In addition to that there is the traffic which the Grand Trunk Railway system gathers in Epgland, and on the continent of Europe that is brought across by the line of steamers connected with the Grand Trunk railway, namely the White Star Line. The Grand Trunk will take that and route it via Sarnia or Midland in the summer time. I do not know whether we have been getting any of that at all; it has probably been going via the Canadian Pacific to the coast. Therefore the hon. member will see that when we have control of the Grand Trunk and it is part of the system, if that traffic is all rail, we will send it to North Bay and when it gets to North Bay it will go over the Canadian National system, and when traffic that is gathered in the West by the Canadian National Railway system consigned to points in Ontario and Quebec arrives at North Bay, we can hand it over to the Grand Trunk which will be part of our system, whereas as it is now we are not interested because the Canadian National railway may hand it over to either the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk.

Large portions of it may be handed over to the Canadian Pacific because it is immaterial to the Canadian National whether they hand it over to the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk because the rates are the same, being fixed by the Railway Commission, only they will give it to the road that has the shortest haul. A railway always hauls freight as far as it can over its own system, because the rate is divided in proportion to the mileage hauled over each railway.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The difficulty I see is that the man who owns the goods will ship them by the cheapest and most expeditious route. Will not the shippers have entire control of how their goods shall be routed ? The Grand Trunk may have commended itself to them as the cheapest and most direct route, but the management cannot say to a man who is sending a few carloads of goods, say, from Montreal to Vancouver, and who starts those goods from Montreal on the Grand Trunk, " These goods must go all the way by our road." The shipper is at liberty to ship his goods by the most expeditious and cheapest route. Freight is an element that must enter into the price of his goods, and he will certainly take care to get the cheapest freight possible. It is not in the power of the Grand Trunk or any other railway to say by what route those goods shall go, unless the freight and transportation facilities are of such a nature as to commend themselves to the judgment of the shipper. So all the advantages which the minister contemplates may not accrue. It will depend entirely on the facilities which the road is capable of affording, its freight rate, and generally its capacity to overcome the competition of other lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Whether the goods are shipped by the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern or thfe Canadian Pacific, the freight rate is exactly the same. That is fixed by the Board of Railway Commissioners. A carload of goods from Montreal to Vancouver will cost the same in freight, if it goes by an all-rail route, no matter by what road it travels. Similarly, if it goes by lake-and-rail,-by rail, for instance, to Sarnia, Midland, Goderich or Owen Sound, Jfien by water to Port Arthur, then by rail again. The lake-and-rail route is a little cheaper than the all-rail, route. What I was trying to point out was this: The Grand Trunk's agent at Montreal, for instance, canvasses a shipper and gets a carload of freight for Vancouver. Now it is very seldom that a shipper says that the goods
[Mr. J. D. Reid.3
must be shipped by Grand Trunk and Canadian Northern, or by Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific. All the shipper cares about is to get his freight to its destination as quickly as possible. The Grand Trunk would carry the freight as far as it could on its own line. The distance to Sarnia, for instance, would be longer than to North Bay, and it would be to the advantage of the Grand Trunk to send the freight as far as possible over its own line in order to get a larger proportion of the freight, which, of course, depends upon the mileage. The shipper is not very much interested in how his goods are routed, because the freight on all three roads is the same. When we get control of the Grand Trunk our railways will all work together, and it will be to our interest to see that the goods, go all the way to their destination by the Government system. I agree that if a shipper wanted to do it, he could direct that his goods he routed by the Grand Trunk to North Bay, and then by Canadian Pacific to Vancouver, and he would get the same freight rate, but it is very seldom a shipper wants that done. It is the railway company that generally advises the shipper, in order that it may get a long haul over its own system. When we take over this road we shall get a very much larger portion of the traffic than we get now.

speechtext:
This is a particularly objectionable clause. The Bill seems to get worse and worse as we proceed. Let me read the clause:
The Government may lend to the said Committee of Management, upon the notes or other obligations of the Grand Trunk, such sums as the Government may from time to time deem necessary to the carrying on or operation of the Grand Trunk system.
See what this clause means. The Committee of Management, is to be composed of five gentlemen, two of whom are friends of the company, two of whom are friends of the Government-and the Minister of the Interior has assured us to-night that these four friends will be so much of one mind that it is not necessary to indicate any means whereby the fifth shall be chosen. This section proposes that the Government, without coming to Parliament for any right to do so, may lend this committee any sums they wish for any purpose that the committee think necessary for the improvement of the road or for the carrying on of its operations Who are "the Government"? Clause 2 throws a little light on vrho may be meant by "the Government" :
Subject to the provisions of this Act, His Majesty the King, represented by the Minister of Railways and Canals of Canada, acting under the authority of the Governor in Council (here-, inafter called the " Government '') ;
In other words the Government is the Minister of -Railways and Canals, to all intents and purposes. This clause says that the Minister of Railways and Canals may, out of the treasury, lend to these five gentlemen, any money that is needed for the purpose of carrying on the operation or improvement of the Grand Trunk system.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Under the authority of an Order in Council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, if you -wish it so. That simply leaves it to Council, on the suggestion or recommendation of the minister himself. If Parliament *wishes to part -with the last vestige of the control that it has over the executive, we should pass this clause, but if Parliament wishes to retain any control it may have over expenditures this clause should not be permitted to stand. If money is needed for the carrying on or improvement of the Grand Trunk system, let the minister come to Parliament, just as the Government does in regard to other appropriations that may be necessary, state in Parliament what money he needs and have that money voted by Parliament. I do not think it is too strong a term to say that this section is thoroughly vicious in that it deprives Parliament altogether of its control over the supplies that may be necessary for this purpose. Under this term " the operation or improvement of the Grand Trunk system " the minister can spend public money for any conceivable purpose in connection with these roads, building hotels, branch lines and stations; he can go into any constituency in this Dominion where the railway is going to run and find that this particular town needs this improvement or that particular county needs that improvement and give the assurance that Parliament has given him the right to lend the company any money it pleases to spend for the purpose of carrying on those improvements. As my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) remarks, a few weeks ago there was a characteristic illustration of this. We saw a letter in one of the journals published in Kingston by a prospective candidate in the approaching election there stating that in view of what had been told him by friends of what was alleged to have been said by the Minister of Railways and Canals as to what /would be done in Kingston, it was useless for him to run as a candidate, that therefore he would withdraw, and as a result the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) was returned unopposed. That kind of thing.is possible under this clause. Nothing can be more subversive of the rights of Parliament and the interests of the people than that any such wholesale power should be given to the Government.

Why cannot the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) be fair in this matter? Why does he not give the whole story? What does the letter which has been read by that hon, gentleman say? speechtext: Let me say at once to my hon. friend that I would be the last person not to accept the statement he had made at the present .moment. I certainly do accept it and I am very glad to do so. I had no other thought in reading the letter than to answer my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) who raised a concrete question, and in regard to this very matter of the campaign in Kingston. We have now disposed of the Kingston incident-a mere side show, which may have been entertaining, -let us now get back to the real question. If there is any principle which is recognized in British parliamentary institutions it is that the appropriation of public moneys is the function of the House of Commons. This section is a flagrant departure from the first principle of British parliamentary government. The Minister of Railways could not get a five-dollar bill to meet the current expenses of his department without bringing down an estimate to this House, and very properly so. Now, what does this clause propose? It reads:
The Government may lend to the said Committee of Management, upon the notes or other obligations of the Grand Trunk, such sums as the Government may from time to time deem necessary for the carrying on of the operation or improvement of the Grand Trunk system.
How long this committee is to remain at work is only an incidental question; it is not vital to us here. The Minister of the Interior practically says that the operations of the committee will extend over a period of at least nine months, and he will not be surprised if it is longer. We all know that operations of this kind move very slowly, and I should not be surprised if this committee remained in charge for a considerable time. We are all anxious to stand by the rights of the House of Commons. Surely it is not unreasonable to say to the Government: Strike out this clause, and if you want any money for the purposes suggested, come down with your estimates and let us vote it the same as
we do for anything else. What reason in the world can be given for giving the Government a blank cheque in regard to this work for the operation, management and improvement-"improvement," you will note-of the Grand Trunk system? My hon. friend says that, he would not start to build hotels; I suppose he wants to wait to know whether the hotels are to be "wet" or "dry." I hope that the Government will not seriously press this clause; I submit in all earnestness and in no party spirit that we ought to stand for the rights of the House of Commons. I ask the Government to reflect seriously before they attempt- to put-a clause like this before the House.

I am not in a position to say what could be fairly estimated; nor, indeed, am I in a position 'to say that, it is possible just at this time to make an- estimate; but I do not think it is unreasonable that the Government should be required to fix a limit beyond which the moneys of the country could not be used for the operation of the road. Not only is it important that we should have the agreement before us so that we may know the date fixed for the valuation of the stock, but we are also interested in over 2,000 miles of railway within the United States. We are also interested in obligations held by the different provinces of Canada. The Grand Trunk lias given certain guarantees for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk Pacific has given certain guarantees for branch lines, in which the provinces are concerned. We see by the press that there is a difference of opinion in regard to these obligations between this Government and the provinces.
Coming back to the United States, I have here some figures which I should like the Government to confirm. The capital of the Central Vermont railway is $2,984,600, of which the Grand Trunk railway owns $2,191,000. The outstanding funded debt is $11,750,000. The Grand Trunk guarantee interest on the bonds providing for deficiency up to 30 per cent of gross receipts on interchange of business. The Central Vermont railway also owns stocks and bonds of the Southern New England railway, which was projected and partly built from Palmer, Mass., to Providence, R.I., but the road has been abandoned. The Central Vermont railway have made advances on account of this line of about $10,000,000, which they are carrying on the asset side of their balance sheet under " Advances ", This money has been lost, and there are now pending suits for breach of contract and damages on account of the abandonment. I understand that a suit is now pending for $3,000,000, and it would be' well to know what responsibility we shall have in connection with that suit. We are embarking upon an undertaking that runs through different states. The state of Maine has issued an order compelling the subsidiary company of the Grand Trunk running through that state to put in a block signal system within a limited time. Only a small part of that work has been done. If we take over that line, that will be an obligation on the part of the Dominion. I think it would be well for us to have the agreement before us so that we shall know our exact relationship to all these undertakings in connection with which there are obligations under state legislation, but of which there is no record in the blue-book. Certain obligations have been laid on the

road which have not yet been carried out, and for which we shall become responsible when we take over the road.

We have hitherto referred generally to the " Grand Trunk System " but to prevent any misunderstanding as to the meaning of that term there will be inserted in the agreement of arbitration below referred to the necessary definition of the term and a statement of how the various companies and their undertakings are controlled by the parent company-whether by stock ownership and to what extent, leases, agreements or otherwise, distinguishing in these respects the direot ownership and control by the parent company and its indirect ownership or control through companies included in the system.
The agreement as contemplated by that clause must provide fully for a more detailed definition of all the various and intricate relationships between the component parts of the Grand Trunk system, including a clear statement of all the obligations in respect of each. I have no personal knowledge of the special obligation which appears to be in dispute with relation to the Southern New England Railway. It is because of the necessity of getting all these matters embodied in the agreement in clearly defined form that it takes some time to prepare the agreement. These matters must all be before the arbitrators and be taken into account by them. Suppose it should turn out that that obligation does exist, and that judgment is recovered against the Central Vermont Railway; that would mean just so much more liability for the Central Vermont Railway, and that much less value in its stock, which, of course, would be reflected in less value in the stock of the Grand Trunk itself.
Consequently the whole transaction as now proposed sees to it that if the stock is reduced .in value we do not pay for it, to that extent. I cannot give further information as to the rights or wrongs of the obligation to which the hon. gentleman refers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The lawsuit will just take its course as if we did not take over

the property. It will be defended by the defendants in the action. We are not the defendants; I presume, from what the hon. gentleman says that the Central Vermont railway are the defendants. Of course, we are interested in the success or non-success of the suit, but we do not interfere in the conduct of the action. We must trust the management in that regard as in any other. We shall be able to dictate the management but not dictate to the management.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: How can the minister pretend that the defendants will be the same persons under public ownership? If the Government owns the railway, in this lawsuit the Government will be substituted for the present defendants, and if they are not, the only inference can be that it is not a question of public ownership.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I hardly know how to put the answer, because I do not like putting it exactly the same way every time, but still there is only one right answer. The ownership of the stock, even of the Grand Trunk, does not change the entity of the company, which is just the same as it was before. It can sue and be sued just the same. Much less-at all events a little less-would the ownership of the stock of the Grand Trunk, the parent company, affect the entity or identity of a subsidiary company. In the same way, we own the stock of the Canadian National railways, and among the subsidiary companies the component parts of that system are the Canadian Northern railway and the Canadian Northern Quebec railway. The Canadian Northern railway is frequently sued the same as any other railway, and so is the Canadian Northern Quebec. The Government does, not rush to the defence of the Canadian Northern; that concern takes care of its own defence. And it will" be just the same with the Central Vermont railway or any other of the component parts of this system.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If a judgment is given against the Canadian Northern, who pays?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Canadian Northern.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But the people of Canada are the Canadian Northern; they are the owners of the stock. Surely if this suit in the United States is pending, and at the time we take the road over an adverse judgment is given, it is plain enough, by whatever name you choose to call the company, the treasury of Canada will be responsible for the amount of the judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I said a moment ago that we were certainly interested in the success or non-success of the suit.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: "Interested" is a mild word.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We are interested as stockholders of the company. If my hon. friend owns stock in a company against which there is a lawsuit, does not the company take care of its own defence? The hon. gentleman does not employ separate counsel, because he is a stockholder, to help the company out. It is just the same here. We do not dictate to them in relation to that part of the management any more than in relation to any other question. We are certainly affected by the judgment the same as stockholders of any company are affected by a lawsuit in which the company is engaged.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says we would not dictate. All we would do is pay the bill.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: According to the minister, the only interest the Government will have in the railways is that of an ordinary shareholder to the extent of the stock held.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Then what about public ownership?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We own all the stock and are interested to that extent, but that does not prevent the company from taking care of itself.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If I hold shares in a company for $200 or $1,000, I am certainly interested in the company, but I cannot contend that I own the company, and the Government to-day claim that the only interest they will have in the system, if this Bill goes through and the agreement is signed, will be the ordinary interest of a shareholder. How can they then contend that the question before Parliament is one of public as against private ownership?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had a little stock he would be a little interested, and if he had all the stock he would be very much interested in the company, but still he would be only a stockholder of the company. The same is true of the Government.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I would like to call the attention of the minister to subsection (a) of section 9. The agreement is to provide for:
(a) the appointment of the arbitrators, the control of the arbitration proceedings; the administration of oaths, etc.
Can we in that way confer the power to administer oaths? Is that the form it should take ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We certainly can if the statute authorizes it.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But does the statute authorize it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, it says so here. The statute authorizes us to do that by agreement.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: By section 9?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is that all?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, the statute says:
The said agreement shall provide, among other necessary and usual provisions	 the administration of oaths.
I do not know what the draughtsman had in mind. I presume it would be that the agreement would provide that oaths could be administered by the arbitrators themselves, and would provide that oaths must be administered before any evidence is taken, or that possibly there should be exceptions to that rule. It is to enable the agreement to provide either for exceptions or no exceptions, and to enable the arbitrators to administer oaths.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I quite understand that it is necessary that the arbitrators should have that power, but the suggestion I offer is that I douibt if this creates on the part of the arbitrators the power to administer oaths-that an incidental reference to it in the agreement may not be sufficient for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Section 10 would meet the difficulty that the hon. gentleman sees.
The Government and the Grand Trunk, and each company comprised in the Grand Trunk system, and all persons interested therein, are hereby respectively authorized and empowered to enter into the said agreement upon and subject to the terms herein set forth, and to do and perform all such acts and things as may he deemed necessary to observe, perform and comply fully with the terms and conditions of said agreement.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

Still, I would ask my hon. friend to consider this in face of the fact that the power to administer an oath

is usually given in a direct form. I must not undertake to teach law to my hon. friend, but I am only asking him to consider whether he thinks that subsection (a) of section 9 creates on the part of the arbitrators the power to administer an oath. I do not think it does.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

I would think myself
that it did. I will ask that that point be reviewed by the legal adviser of the Government. In the meantime the clause need not be postponed, because if it is found that there is the difficulty apprehended by my hon. friend we can revert to it later.

Just a moment. I wish to call the attention of the minister to paragraph (d) of section 9. We have been told a good many times that the receiver was under the control of the Exchequer Court. Now we are taking that control ou't of the power of the court and telling the receiver what he shall do. I do not think that is good practice. Under the prevailing practice the receiver is under the control of the court in which he is and he cannot move very much without the direction of the court. Now I suppose if the minister goes to the judge of the Exchequer Court and asks for an order telling him to do whatever is necessary under this Bill he will get that order and get that direction; but by this Bill we are taking the matter out of the judge's hands entirely and putting it back into the hands of the Governor iri Council. I submit, it is very irregular that part of their proceedings shall be subject to the decision of the Exchequer Court judge and that something

else shall be in the hands of the Governor in Council. We were told it was taken out of the hands of the Governor in Council and was under the control of the judge. I do not agree with this practice that part of the proceedings should be taken out and part of it left, when it is perfectly clear that the minister will get whatever order he may get from the judge himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
This clause provides
that the agreement shall contain the terms looking to the passing of the receivership from the Minister of Railways to the Committee of Management to the end that the Grand Trunk Pacific may be run as part of the Grand Trunk system. Now, of course the agreement can only do what the parties to the agreement are able to do, that is to say, what the Government can do on its part and the Grand Trunk on the part of the other side; they cannot override the Exchequer Court. I would say that the approval of the Exchequer Court judge would be necessary in order that the terms of the agreement in that regard should be effective. The receiver being empowered as between himself and the shareholders of the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific to transfer the receivership to the Committee of Management he would also have to go to the Exchequer Court to get the approval of the judge. I think that would follow as a matter of law; it would not be required to be stated here.

On section 10-Authority for Government, Grand Trunk companies, and all parties interested, to enter into agreement:

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does the minister think that the sections of the systems, or the companies, which now compose and will hereafter compose part of the sysitem, and which are within the limits of the United States, require parliamentary authority to enter into this agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Well, of course the effedt of this clause cannot go any further than it is within the jurisdiction of Parliament to legislate with regard to, say an American road. I do not know that we could legislate with regard to anything concerning it. All we say here is, that agreement is executed between, the Grand Trunk Company and .the Government. It may be there shall be some other companies made parties to the agreement. That may be found necessary. But so far as we have power to say to these companies, the parties to the agreement: " You shall be able to do what that agreement provides you shall do," we say it. If we have not power, then, of course, there is nothing added to it at all and there is no harm done. We can simply do this to the extent of our jurisdiction.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Well, I think it would be good drafting and good legislation to say that we are only legislating within our jurisdiction. But that was only within my mind as a secondary thought; I asked the minister if he thought that when these American companies-American in name and American in location-are joining in this agreement they require statutory or parliamentary authority to <lo so. If they do they would have to go to the legislatures of the respective states in which they are located for that authority; and I wish to ask the minister if he is providing for a con-

tingency of that kind, that those companies -for instance in the state of Massachusetts or the state of Maine-would go to their respective state legislatures for authority to enter into this agreement? Where it is perfectly clear that we cannot give them authority, they being beyond the zone of our jurisdiction, it would look better for us to say in this section that we are only legislating within the confines of Canada and within the jurisdiction of this Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

We do not think there is the slightest possibility that any American company would require any enlargement of their power for anything they would have to do.

I am told that that information has not been wholly secured as yet, but I think it would meet the hon. gentleman's object if I say that the company operates its Pullman cars under a long-term contract expiring in 1937, by the terms of which the Pullman Company get a certain proportion of
11 p.m. the revenue derived from the operation of these cars, commencing after the Grand Trunk gets a fixed proportion. That is the nature of the agreement; the exact details as to the amounts I am not able to give as yet.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

That was a contingency which the draftsman had in mind; I'myself cannot see that it will likely eventuate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-Orders in Council authorized to vest in Government any preference or common stocks not transferred, or to vacate office of director, or otherwise to* carry out agreement.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: This section professes to vest in the Governor in Council power to deal with the stock of this company wherever it may be. We are professing to pass an order cancelling the powers which a man who lives in Switzerland has by virtue of the terms of a stock certificate of this company which he holds-a certificate which is personal property and cannot be affected in any way, except as to the value of the stock, by what becomes of the rails and cars here. I submit that when a person who owns a property and the property itself is beyond the jurisdiction of this Parliament, we cannot legislate in regard to one or the other. I suppose it is no harm to pass the section as it is, but I do not think we are giving to the minister the power that- the language of the section would indicate.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Is not the drafting of this section peculiar? The first two lines read:
Any orders of the Governor in Council which the Government may deem requisite to vest in the Government.
The ordinary form would be that "the Governor in Council" -may do certain things. "The Government" is defined at an earlier stage as meaning the Minister of Railways, but the distinction between 'Government" and "Governor in Council" in this clause seems to be inconvenient.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I really think that the hon. gentleman is right. I move that this clause be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
The Governor in Council may make such orders as are deemed requisite to vest in the

Government any of the preference or common stocks not transferred to the Government or its nominees under the terms of this Act, or to vacate any office of director, or otherwise to carry into effect the terms and provisions of the said agreement.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What is the meaning of the words "its nominees"? Is it the intention that this stock, instead of being vested in the Minister of Eailways-that is, the Government-may be vested in somebody else nominated by the .minister,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The idea, I think, is, to vest, it in the Minister of Finance instead of in His Majesty represented by the Minister of Railways, as the words "the Government" are, in effect, defined.
On section 12-discharge of receivership of Grand Trunk Pacific and termination of proceedings in Exchequer Court.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I really think we have made excellent progress to-day. There is some information that should be given in connection with this clause and that will take a little too long to give to-night. Speaking for myself, I have not been able to grasp exactly our relations to the Grand Trunk Pacific, what the Grand Trunk Pacific owes to the people of Canada and how that obligation is to be discharged^ in connection with this agreement. I think that would all come into play under this section. I would be glad if the minister would let this clause stand until to-morrow and be prepared then to give a full explanation of what our relations are. Although the matter has been referred to incidentally several times, I do not think a full explanation has "been given and it would not take ten minutes to give one. Speaking for myself, I should like to have that explanation before we leave this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: As to what the Grand Trunk Pacific owes to the Government?

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, and how it is proposed to satisfy that obligation. The minister -told me long ago in connection with this discussion that the Grand Trunk would have to pay whatever the obligation was, but other ministers said that it would not be so. For instance, the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) early in the discussion made a speech in which he said that we forced the Grand Trunk into this agreement and that we should deal sympathetically with them in connection with this obligation. But the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) said, as he will find 
by reference to his speech in the early stages of the discussion, that the money would have to be paid. We would like to know definitely what line of procedure is to be taken, how the amount, directly and indirectly owed, is to be definitely ascertained and how it is to be paid. Are any terms to be put into this agreement by which the arbitrators can deduct that amount from the final award that they may make, leaving us to pay only what will he due to the Grand Trunk after all their liabilities have been satisfied so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned?

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I do not wish to be
hypercritical, but again may I direct the minister's attention to the form of drafting of clause 12, which reads:
Upon the transfer to or vesting in the Government of the preference and common stock as herein provided for, the Government-
Which means according to my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways as representing His Majesty the King.
.-may, by order in council provide

That is to say, the Minister of Railways is the boss, and he may direct the Governor in Council to do things. I do not think this is good practice.	,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The drafting is entirely wrong there. It should read:
The Governor in Council may provide-
Just as the hon. member has suggested in reference to clause 11.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Meighen moves
to amend clause 12 by striking out the word " Government " in the third line thereof and the words " by Order in Council " in the same line and to replace the word " Government " by the words " Governor in Council" so that the clause will read:
Upon the transfer to or vesting in the Government of the preference and common stock as herein provided for, the Governor in Council may provide for the discharge of the receiver-snip of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System and the termination and withdrawal of the proceedings in the Exchequer Court of Canada relating thereto.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Had you not better
say " by Order in Council?"

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
