speechtext:
That is not necessary.
That is the only way in which they can provide it I have no objection to meeting the request of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) as regards letting this clause stand. I can only add that the debts that the Grand Trunk Pacific owe to the Government and

the debts that the Grand Trunk owe to the Government are all set out in the agreement, and that all that I have ever said is that all those obligations must be taken into account by the arbitrators. What the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) may have said when I did not have the pleasure of hearing him, I do not know, but he has had a full understanding and has made a careful study of this question, and I should be very much surprised if he has said anything different from what I have said.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does the minister now say that this will be dealt with as a business transaction between two business concerns; that any money or obligations that the Grand Trunk Pacific owe or must discharge to the people of Canada will be fully considered and properly dealt with? But there is something else that I forgot. There are large claims against the Grand Trunk Pacific other than our claims. When we take over this road we are taking over not only the obligations to ourselves but the obligations to other people from whom the Grand Trunk Pacific borrowed money and who hold the stocks and bonds of that company; some of those guaranteed by us, some guaranteed by the Grand Trunk and some not guaranteed at all, but all of them claims against the road. I will expect the minister to explain to-morrow where we stand, when we take over this road as we are making provision under clause 12 to do, as to the different obligations, not only our own claims against the road but the various other claims that stand against it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I will promise to make to-morrow in that regard the same explanation as I have made repeatedly before, and, I hope, as clearly.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not remember that we ever dealt with the obligations and claims of other creditors of the road than ourselves; at least I was not here when they were dealt with. I have not heard any explanation in regard to that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They are given. There is, however, no objection to postponing the consideration of this clause. As to the hon. gentleman's request to be informed whether this matter will be dealt with in a business way, I have not distinctly said so because in relation to this Government, that always goes without saying.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If I may be permitted, I would like to ask a question in regard to the property investment in road and equipment. The amount, as appears on page 38 of the blue-book, is $434,990,999.37. This question may have been answered before, and if so I might be referred to where it was answered, and that will be satisfactory to me. On what basis was that amount arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Actual cost of road and equipment. I may say that in all probability the equipment is worth considerably more than cost. An estimate believed to be reasonable was given by the Minister of Railways about two days ago in which estimate the equipment end of this figure was estimated to stand now at about $180,000,000.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is, it is not the physical valuation at the time this statement was made out?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, the actual cost.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Has the depreciation been taken from the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No, I do not think depreciation is taken off. If you take off depreciation you would have to add appreciation, and if so, I think you would have a much larger amount than this.
Section as amended, stands.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Some time ago I drew the attention of the Minister of Railways to the position in which the cwities and other municipalities and school authorities receiving taxes from these roads would be when the roads become the property of the Government. I said that being government property they would be exempt from local taxation. Thus this measure will be an interference with the taxes now collected by these different bodies. I am in receipt for my information of a copy of the following letter from Mr. Harold Fisher, Mayor of the city of Ottawa:
The Honourable J. D. Reid, M.P.,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:-I am the president of the Union of Canadian Municipalities.
This Union has been instructed to request that the Grand Trunk Railway Bill shall contain a clause preserving the right of municipalities to tax the property of the railway and to protest against the passing of the Bill without a clause of this kind being inserted. The Union has been officially asked to take this stand 'by the following cities-Montreal, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Quebec, Galt, Chatham, and St. John's, P.Q. Unofficially this position has been approved by Toronto and many other places and will, no doubt, be followed by official action.



Herewith I am enclosing a clause drafted by the city of (Montreal. X am not sure that the wording of this clause is the best possible, but it will serve to give you the idea of the municipalities.
I am taking the liberty of sending a copy of this letter to some of your colleagues and to some other members of the House.
Tours truly,
(Sgd.) Harold Fisher.
To meet the wishes of the Union of Canadian Municipalities I now beg to move to add to the Bill as clause 13 the following:
Nothing in this Act or any amendments thereof shall diminish or prejudice the effect of any right of assessment or taxation now or hereafter appertaining to any municipality' or municipal institution over and upon the property or income of the railway or any of its subsidiaries, branches or accessories.
If this clause is not correctly worded I would a&k the minister to have it put in proper form, so that the municipal authorities will be satisfied. There is more than the ordinary municipal tax involved; the school tax may also be affected. I trust the minister will come to the conclusion that a clause to the above effect should be inserted in the Bill for the protection of the municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I thoroughly approve of the result which the hon. gentleman thinks so much desirable, namely, that the right of any municipality to assess and tax now enjoyed should not be interfered with. I thoroughly approve of that, notwithstanding that some reflections were cast upon it by the leader of the Opposition yesterday, but there is no need of an amendment to bring that about. Manifestly that is brought about already. There is nothing in this Act that would in any way affect the right of any municipality to tax. This is an Act to acquire some stock. The position of a municipality in relation to the company is just the same after we get the stock as before we get it. So manifestly there is no need of the amendment. It would be mere surplusage and be rather indefensible, I think, to add it. You might just as well enact that nothing in this Act should result in the annexation of taxes or vary the transit of Venus. So why add the amendment? Apparently there has been some systematic attempt to convince municipalities that a raid was being made on their rights, and they have sent down petitions. Let the hon. gentlemen join with me in assuring the municipalities that as the Act stands their riglits are not affected in the slightest degree. That is all the assurance they need.
	,

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
What position will the
towns on the Transcontinental, for instance, be in with regard to taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Exactly the same position they are in now.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What is that position?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Government owns
the Transcontinental as a property. I might observe that when this transaction is consummated the Government will own just the same properties it owns to-day, no more and no less, except one thing: it will physically own the stock of ' the Grand Trunk railway. That stock, as stock, will not be taxable because we own it. It never has been taxable here anyway. The position of the municipalities will be exactly the same as it is to-day.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that the towns on the Transcontinental are in a different position from towns on the Grand Trunk, because they will have to pay their share of the deficits, if any, but will not be in a position to tax the portion of the system that is earning the dividends.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They are in that position now. They will be in exactly the same position after this legislation passes.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: When the Grand Trunk is added to the Government system municipalities in one portion of the country will have the right to tax what the Government is pleased to call the Government-owned railways, while municipalities in another portion of the country will not have that right. Is that fair? All the municipalities have to help make up any deficits by contributing as individuals to the treasury of the country, but some of the municipalities are not in a position to tax part of the Government system.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We are not putting them in that position at all. That is the position they are in to-day.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend will admit that he is putting them in the position of having to pay their portion of the deficit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
When the Grand Trunk Pacific was built it was built by a company with Government assistance. The whole country had to contribute to the erection of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the municipalities along the line could tax it. As regards the Transcontinental, the money of the whole country went into that, but the municipalities along the line could not tax it, although they had to contribute. So that

situation has existed. If there is any unfairness in that respect there has been just the same unfairness heretofore. The situation has not been altered in the slightest degree.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Except that the municipalities along the Transcontinental will have to contribute more to the deficits of the Canadian National railway. They will have to contribute their portion as individuals, and they will have no right as a municipality to tax the road because it happens to be public-owned instead of private-owned. My hon. friend at least will not argue that they are in a fair position when they have to contribute in taxation towards the deficits on the national undertaking, but have not the right to tax the railway.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the position of the municipalities be changed after thirty years if the Government decides to redeem the outstanding stock?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister has just explained that property owned to-day by the Grand Trunk will in the future, as in the past, be taxable by the municipalities and also by the school commissions. What about property acquired or built in the future? Suppose, for instance, the Grand Trunk builds a new station in Levis; would it be subject to taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It would be subject to taxation under the new conditions if it would have been subject to taxation under the old.
For example, suppose this transaction does not take place at all and two years from now the Grand Trunk railway build a station at Levis. If it is the law that that station is taxable it will be taxable just the same whether we own the stock or not.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister said he understood that the Grand Trunk Pacific was subject to taxation by the municipalities through which it passed. I got a return from the Government in answer to a question I asked on this matter in which I requested information as to the amount of municipal taxes paid by the Grand Tr.unk system, the Canadian Northern system, and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The minister was kind enough to send me a memorandum containing the following information :	.
Grand Trunk	$654,736.22
Canadian Northern	 206,627.20
Grand Trunk Pacific.. .. Nothing.
Will the minister reconcile this statement with what he said a moment ago?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The explanation is this, and it applies to Manitoba and other provinces through which the Grand Trunk Pacific runs. These provinces abrogated the right of municipalities to tax and substituted in its place a tax to the province itself on a basis fixed in provincial legislation. Consequently there is no municipal tax but a tax paid to the province instead. Then,-although this does not really appertain very much to the question-numerous exemptions of taxation were granted.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am astonished at the answer given by the Minister of the Interior in connection with the ownership of these different roads which will come under the Government's control. We are going to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we are told that we own every inch of the Canadian Northern. When we take over the Grand Trunk system it is true we shall own it in the name of the company, but that does not mean anything at all in equity and fairness. We shall be holding the system under the name of a company that is to all intents and purposes defunct. In reality it will be owned by the people of Canada. The same thing applies to every other road which we say we own; it is exactly the position in regard to the Intercolonial railway and the Transcontinental railway. Our owning these concerns in the names of companies is absolutely a fiction of law. Some of these railroads which are owned by the people will pay taxes, but the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental will not. Where is the fairness in that? The farmer in Prince Edward Island will pay his share of the deficit on the entire sysitem, but he gets no taxes at all. He must pay his school rates the same as if these roads were not owned by the people. The farmer of Ontario pays his share of deficit, but he gets his school rates and municipal rates and every other assessable rate out of the railway. The same Government owns these different roads and it is not fair that such discrimination should be made. The people of the country will not be satisfied with such conditions.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is not the Intercolonial Railway itself a corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The title of the Intercolonial is in the Crown

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Before it was transferred to the Government railways it was.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Intercolonial does not pay dividends?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Prior to the war it did.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Under this Act the dividends will gb to the shareholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They will go to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Surely the minister is not serious in making the statement that the dividends go to the people of Canada?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Order. This interruption by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was irrelevant. It has nothing to do with the question now before the committee, and I hope the committee will not recommence a discussion concerning public ownership.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the Government seriously consider making some provision so that the people along the Intercolonial and Transcontinental lines may have the privilege of taxing the railway the same as people along other portions of government-owned roads? I do not think that there should be any discrimination to the detriment of certain towns.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am not very much impressed by the hon. gentleman's argument, but even if I were I do not see that there should be any discussion on the subject in relation to this Bill. If it were thought proper to do that later on, it could be done. I said I was not much impressed by the contention of the hon. member, but I do not see that my impression matters one way or the other.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Not to me.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I know that; I know there are other considerations that matter much more to the hon. member. Getting down to the merits of the question, in the first place, there is nothing discriminatory in connection with present conditions as against the Maritime Provinces. The Transcontinental runs from east to west. It is not taxable because it is owned by the Crown. Now, I suppose hon. members contend that because we own the stock in companies that operate certain railways we must therefore go to the Intercolonial and make that government property taxable. I cannot see any connection in the reasoning at all. The same trend of reasoning would carry you on to post offices and you would have to make them taxable because the people that use post offices contribute

to the deficit on the Intercolonial or the Transcontinental or on the Grand Trunk Pacific, or wherever a railway happens to pass through.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does the minister say that some post offices are taxable and others are not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No, but the same argument that would lead you to the conclusion that because we own the stock of the Grand Trunk we must remove exemption from taxation on the Intercolonial would lead you to the argument in respect to the post offices.
The same .argument applies in the one case as in the other except that one is called a railway and the other is called a post office. Then there is the further consideration that in relation to these companies their property is now taxable. Many municipalities have bonused these companies to come in, one reason being that they could tax their properties. Nobody bonuses a Government road to come in. The logic of the situation drives me to the conclusion that as there is no injustice in the present conditions a continuance of those conditions will be no injustice either.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister tells us
that we are in the position of ordinary stockholders in so far as the Grand Trunk is concerned when we come to own the stock. The worst thing that can happen the ordinary stockholder is that he gets no dividend on his stock. He owes no money to the company,, he has bought his stock and he has it in his possession. Our position is that if the Grand Trunk makes a loss we not only get no dividend on our stock but we must pay for that loss.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly, the Government will have to pay the shortage or deficit, as it pays the deficit on the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern and the Intercolonial. Any shortage in connection with this company will come out of the revenues of the people. It is fallacious in the highest degree to say we are only in the position of stockholders.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We are exactly in the same position as stockholders are in relation to any company. We are not responsible for the deficits on the Grand Trunk. It is true the Grand Trunk must borrow. If there are further deficits, the Government lends the road money and the company pays its own debts. But we are in hopes that there will be a surplus in time.

subsubtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
There are several reasons which I desire to suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, why I think this motion is not timely. In the first place, I think I am correct in stating that it is a kind of motion which, in the experience of Parliament, is never made except at the end of a long and laborious session. Under some circumstances, at the end of such a session there is justification for pressure of this kind. But we have not yet reached the end of a long and laborious session. We have not yet passed the second month of the session, and that is only about half the time

that a session. usually occupies. I have not looked up the records, but I am relying on my own experience and recollection when I say that I think my hon. friend will have difficulty in finding a case where a motion of this kind was made in the second month of the session. The second point I desire to make is this: When we made representations, or when it was alleged that a very important measure was being pressed through the House with what we thought was undue haste, the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) replied that there would be no undue haste, no undue hurry, no intention of departing from the regular order of business and that there would be abundant time allowed for the consideration of the measure. My hon. friend was perhaps not in the House when that assurance was given, but there was the promise and declaration of the Government that there would be no unusual proceeding, no hurry, no rush and that there would be an abundance of time. I claim that the motion that my hon. friend is making is a breach of the understanding that was come to at that time.
Third, the hon. gentleman is proposing that the House shall meet morning, noon and night. He is the oldest member of the House, but I am old enough to know -and we are both old enough to know- that when you attempt to hold meetings of this Parliament morning, noon and night you do not get any intelligent and deliberate judgment on the questions brought before the House. The pressure that is brought to bear on members sitting here morning, noon and night and attending to whatever duties they may have to perform surely unfits them for the effective discharge of their duties. That is something that should only be resorted to under the most urgent conditions. Such conditions have not yet been reached.
Last and more important than all is that I venture to say in the whole of our Canadian parliamentary history my hon. friend will not find that a motion of this kind has ever been made at a moment when the House has not had a single opportunity of discussing the general affairs of this country. We have been dealing with particular subjects. The Peace Treaty is one, the Grand Trunk Bill is another, and on each of these occasions if any member departed from the subject before the House he was very properly called to order and required to confine himself to that particular subject. That is a necessary, and proper rule of Parliament, but if it is a
necessary and proper rule it has to be accompanied by another, and that is that there shall be abundant opportunity for discussing the affairs of the country generally on the motion to go into Committee of Supply. We have now reached the end of the second month of this session and we have not yet had that opportunity by a motion being made to refer the Estimates to the Committee of Supply. Indeed, we have' not yet had any Estimates. I asked the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) the other day if there would be any Estimates and he said: "Yes, there are going to be some Estimates; they will come along shortly." I say in all seriousness 'that the right to discuss public affairs generally on the motion for supply is one of the most valuable privileges we enjoy under the British parliamentary system. That is purposely designed to afford a wide opportunity of discussing' all questions relating to our public affairs and this is the first time in the history of this Parliament when a motion has been made before there has been any opportunity for such public discussion which is the essence of our parliamentary system. I think my hon. friend, who is an old and experienced parliamentarian, will, on reflection, regard these considerations as abundant reasons why he should not press this motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to be pretty difficult to meet the views of my hon. friends on the other side of the House. They seem to have different views at different times with no very long time between their exceedingly different views. It is true that this motion is being made, compared with other sessions of Parliament, at a comparatively earlier period than is usual in the regular sessions but if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) will take into consideration that this is a special session and that no very considerable length of session was anticipated I think he will be disposed to take a different view of the matter. If he will make a comparison as to the time of the introduction of such a motion as this in connection with the circumstance I have alluded to, the short session for which we had been summoned, he will find that relatively the .motion is as well advanced in point of time as during normal sessions when it has been introduced at a later period; that is to say more days after the commencement of the session. That is in reference to my hon. friend's first reason.
The second reason, that he gives, is weakened by this consideration:	Parliament does not consider it to be a good

business to meet when committees are in session because a large proportion of the most important business of the House is done in committee. The committees have practically finished all their business at this time. The members therefore have no call upon their time to attend the sessions of these committees in the forenoon and the conditions are not the same as they were when they had that ca!l. We are simply asking the member of Parliament to come and deliberate upon or consider matters in this House when in a normal session he would be at work in committees. The committees have done their work and the time of the members is at their own disposal. It does not seem to me to be very much to ask them, being relieved of work in the committees, to come to the House of Commons and undertake the consideration of questions which are proper and necessary to be considered in the House itself. I think that these two suggestions I have made take away from the force of my hon. friend's objection. What we are here for, when you come down to basic principles, is to get through with the work of the session. We have not ipushed it by extraordinary methods; we have not used any compulsion at all; we have not hurried up the deliberations of the House, nor have we proposed to do it, but in consideration of the fact that the committees are not sitting, it does not seem to be unreasonable to ask the members to stay in the House and to devo'te all the time which they would otherwise, under normal conditions, give to the committees, to the work in the House.
Then, a word in reference to the programme which seems to have sprung up all at once in the mind of my hon. friend, and which opens up vistas of distance which we did not contemplate before. It seems that my hon. friend feels that at this special session it is incumbent upon him after two months of cogitation to open up the affairs of the country and go into a general discussion of conditions, financial and otherwise. This had not been contemplated at this special session. It is to my mind a question whether it is necessary or wise. I think there would have to be some very strong reasons given as to why a large amount of time should be spent after this in discussing general political conditions because that is about what it would mean, or whether we should finish the necessary business, get to our homes and be prepared to come back at the regular session of Parliament and discuss the affairs of the country. We would have had this purpose, and

this purpose alone, if it had not been for the intervention of a special session called for a special purpose. For that special purpose it has been called and along with it advantage has been taken of the presence of the members here to bring before them a little necessary and urgent legislation for their consideration and opinion.
I do not, as a member of the Government, w'ant to compel members of the House who, on broad principles, h&ve the disposal of their time in their own handsi, to sit in the mornings at this period, if they do not desire to do so; but under the present circumstances, there being no committee work to be performed, we might well add the mornings, which we would otherwise spend in committee work, to the sittings of the House and attend to the business of the country. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) is not much older than I am and he is quite as vigorous. I am quite willing to come morning, afternoon and evening, if it is necessary, in order, in an orderly way, to put the business through; and those young fellows opposite, some of whom have very lately entered Parliament, surely cannot plead physical fatigue against the duty of a member of Parliament.

speechtext: The leader of the Government seems to entertain the idea, or at least has tried to make us believe, that he is presenting the motion with a view of giving satisfaction to members on this side. We certainly are not accustomed to such treatment from the Government side and if true it will be the first time since I have been a member of Parliament that a motion was offered by the Government for the sole purpose of giving satisfaction to the Opposition. I am really surprised that our views should have such weight as to have made such an impression on the leader of the Government. Coming now to the merits of the question, let me say that we have been repeatedly promised by the Minister of the Interior, and other members of the Government, that the Bill for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway, which will be the chief issue before us until the session closes, would not be pressed with any haste whatever, but that all the time necessary should be given members to discuss the measure. We have been debating the Bill for several days and it is now proposed that the House will hold three sittings a day. In my opinion this is equivalent to chloroforming Parliament.

subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I mean what I say, and no one will deny the statement. No member who stays out of the House will be chloroformed, but not a single member can stand three sittings a day. I claim to have been just as assiduous in my attendance here as any other hon. gentleman and physically I am just as strong, but I cannot stand three sittings a day and I would like to hear from any hon. member who can endure that number of sittings and give reasonable and proper consideration to the legislation.'before us and arrive at a well-considered judgment. I do not think that could be said of any member on either side. It has been said, Sir, that this session, having regard to the object for which it was called, was a farce. If at the beginning it was a farce it has now developed
into a very serious matter. We have now been here for two months and the leader of the Government is satisfied that our object has been accomplished, that we have-earned our indemnity and that we should go home. Well, my understanding, to which I propose to adhere, is that full opportunity should be afforded to consider such legislation as is brought down and especially such important legislation as the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. Otherwise, we might as well go home, or remain out of the House, and simply come here to vote when a division takes place. It is an easy matter for hon. gentlemen who were interrupting me a minute ago to say "We are ready to vote and to go home." Let me recall one circumstance to illustrate how these hon. gentlemen regard their parliamentary duties. When the Grand Trunk Bill was introduced by the Minister of the Interior, I saw around him a galaxy of Government supporters who had gathered simply for the purpose of applauding the project. As everybody will acknowledge this measure contains one of the most important propositions that has ever been submitted to Parliament. It is one of the most difficult in its character that we have ever been called upon to consider, and yet these hon. gentlemen have already made up their minds in regard to it. They congregated around the Minister of the Interior and after he had submitted the Bill to the House applauded him. Well, for that kind of work, the House might sit three times a day and even for the whole twenty-four hours; it would not involve any great hardship to hon. gentlemen who had made up their minds in advance. But that is not true of those members who want to form a well-considered judgment with respect to this legislation. They must not only steadfastly attend the sittings -but carefully study the legislation. No man can sit at his desk in this House and do that unless he has had ample opportunity in advance to consider the subject and make up his mind on the provisions of the Bill. I could give many other reasons why this motion should not be entertained, but I know it would be useless. I will simply register my protest against this motion as I will protest against any motion of the same nature which may be submitted to the House in future.

subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
As a western member I want to endorse very heartily the suggestion of the Government that we should get on with the busi-

-ness of the session. It is all very well for 'hon. gentlemen to protest who live in 'Ottawa or whose homes are so near that they can reach them during the "weekly recess to favour delaying the session, but we members who reside in the West and are obliged to remain here month after month, and I think I voice their sentiments, chafe very grievously when any unnecessary delay takes place. As a matter of fact, the commitees have finished their work and members are merely idling about the corridors and the smoking rooms restless because they have in the morning nothing to do. I see no hardship whatever In sitting three times a day and I am much older than my hon. friend who has just spoken. I do not find anything laborious about attending the sessions of Parliament; the trouble is that so many of us at certain hours have nothing at all to do; and if we intervene in a debate we are liable -to be frowned at and charged with speaking too long and unnecessarily taking up "time.
But this is a special session called for a special purpose, and if men who have businesses to look after are to be kept here month after month they will be obliged to retire altogether from politics. Surely the -session has already lasted almost a month longer than we expected.

subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Certainly, because
very important business developed, and I [DOT]take it that members are perfectly willing to remain here until that business is finished. But why we should not occupy the entire day, or most of it, in sitting in the House is more than I can understand. As to. opening up the whole business of the country in connection with the Budget, if we do that we will not need to adjourn at all; there will be no need for an intermission between this and the regular session.
I feel that I express the sentiment of members from the West when I say that while every reasonable courtesy should be extended to the Opposition, no time should be lost in driving the business of the House through in a legitimate manner.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria):
subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
leader of the Government (Sir George Foster), with his usual facility for finding suitable words, twitted us for changing our minds so very often. I think that is one of the things he should not have said, for if there have been any rapid changes about how long the session should last they sure-
lv have their origin with the hon. gentleman himself. It is not more than two or three weeks since he called me to task for suggesting anything but an immediate winding up of the business of the House. He said then, as he says now, that this was a special session called for a special purpose; he intimated that purpose had been fulfilled and the minds of members had been made up that their work was finished and that Parliament should prorogue. We accepted that as the opinion of the hon. gentlemen on that side of the House, ex pressed through their leader; now we find that the hon. gentleman has radically changed his mind. We cannot continue to call the session a special session,' because business far wide of the subject which the session was specially called to consider has been introduced; the session has become one of general import, dealing -generally with the business of the country. The business that is nowr before the House was not in the mind of any members when they came here on the first day of September. We were called here hurriedly for the purpose of dealing with the Peace Treaty. I need not go into the mental philosophy of the thing; my hon. friend knows that when a man makes up his mind to a certain line of action and thinks that a duty that he had in hand is-finished he is not so very ready to throw away that idea and the impression that is on his mind and entirely change his course of action. We have been told by the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) and others that there is plenty of time; that there is no need of chafing under continuous sittings. The leader of the Government knows that if he makes up his mind that he has to stay in a place for a certain number of days and is to go at the end of that time it is not pleasant if he has to stay longer, because, as I have said, he has made up his mind to a certain course of action. But we are now in the midst of this business ; our minds are fully charged with it. We realize the responsibility w'hieh attaches to it and I do not think vre should be hurried too much. The Minister of the Interior has said that there would be no need to hurry; that all possible convenience and time would be at the disposal of members.
Now, the wisdom of the ages has fixed the sittings of Parliament from three o'clock in the afternoon until such hour as we may adjourn. Those are the regular working hours; they have prevailed for the last fifty years in this country, as they have, I think, in the Old Country, and they should not be

departed from without good reason. The hours are so arranged that hon. members may have part of the day for reading and study and for seeking information in connection with the subjects under deliberation. I submit that to go home at ten or twelve o'clock at night and come here at eleven o'clock the next morning and enter upon the grind of sessional work leaves no time for anything of that kind. It is part -of the member's work to read the newspapers. If you see a member reading a newspaper you may think that he is enjoying himself. But that is not the idea; it is a duty; he must read the papers if he wishes to keep in touch with public opinion. The leader of the Government will admit that certain time must be given for that if for nothing else, but under the arrangement suggested there will be no time at all for any of these things.
The Treaty of Peace and the Grand Trunk proposal are very important subjects, but the most important business of the session has not yet been brought before the House. I submit that the question of the re-establishment of the soldier is the most important question-looked upon, at all events, from the humanitarian standpoint-with which we have to deal. The report of the committee is not yet brought down. I have no idea, except from what I have seen in the press, of what the report is going to be. I assume that legislation will be introduced, and that serious consideration is to be given to that question. That alone, I submit, is good reason why at least during the whole of next week we should proceed along the old lines.
The Minister of Railways twitted us rather sarcastically the other night about the desire to go home; he suggested that we were running from work and wanted to go home. It seems that the shoe is on the other foot now; the extreme desire for quitting is on the other side of the House.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
subtopic: DISCUSSION ON MOTION FOR MORNING SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is any good ground for not accepting the resolution, it 'has certainly not been established by hon. gentlemen opposite. In presenting the resolution there is no intention or effort on the part of members of the Government to suit their own convenience, because individually they would much prefer a continuance of the usual
hours. The resolution is merely an honest and sincere effort on the part of the Government to meet what they thought wias the desire of the House. After all, this is a matter for Parliament to settle; if it is the desire of Parliament that we meet during the remainder of the session at three o'clock as usual, the Government will bow to the wishes of hon. members. It has never been officially intimated to the House by the Opposition that they desire an early termination of the session; nevertheless- and I hope I am not violating any principle of propriety when I say this-to me personally and to members on this side individual members opposite have expressed a desire that the 'business of this session he concluded at the earliest possible moment consistent with its being properly considered and dealt with.
After all, the question is: Is there any substantial reason why we should not hereafter meet in the .mornings at eleven o'clock? As has been pointed out by the leader of the House, there is no further committee work. I have never been partial to morning sittings, and I would not favour this resolution if committees were to meet during the balance of the session. I agree with the suggestion entirely; but inasmuch as there will be no further sittings of committees, might not hon. gentlemen as well assemble here at eleven o'clock in the morning, as at three o'clock in the afternoon? Would it not be wiser on our part to put in two hours' work between eleven and one o'clock and endeavour to close at a respectable hour in the evening, say at ten or eleven o'clock? I think that would safeguard the health and comfort of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) better than if we met at three o'clock and sat until twelve or one o'clock at night, and it would afford the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) ample opportunity for reading the newspapers late in the evening, which is the time when all busy men read the newspapers. I do not think it is fair to suggest, as it has been suggested, that this represents an intention on the part of the Government to curtail or minimize debate on the Grand Trunk Bill. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) has given his word to Parliament that every opportunity will he afforded to hon. members in this House to debate that measure, and the Government will adhere to the promise made by that minister. It does not mean that the session will perhaps close any earlier by our meeting at eleven o'clock in

the forenoon; but on the whole, considering the fact that there are no further committee meetings, I think it is for the comfort of members that we should meet at eleven o'clock and endeavour to close at an earlier hour than we have been doing lately. The motion is a fair one, and it is submitted with the sincere desire of meeting what was apparently the wishes of hon. gentlemen, and I am surprised that there is any opposition to it.

On section 12-Discharge of receivership of Grand Trunk Pacific and termination of proceedings in Exchequer Court.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
This seems to be incomplete; it does not say what is to become of the road. Before the receivership the road belonged to a private and independent company, the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Now we propose by this section to put an end to the receivership, but there is nothing to show what becomes of the road. Will the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have absolute control of the property as before the receivership, or is it the intention of the Government to continue it as part of the Government-owned system?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: On the discharge of the receivership the road would go back into the legal position it occupied before the receivership. That is to say, it would be administered by the stockholders of the road.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The stockholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, who are the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Of course, the Government being owners of the stock of the Grand Trunk would necessarily have full supervision and be in absolute control. Thait is all that is wanted.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is it clear from the Bill that provision is made foT then merging it with the Canadian National roads? We all know what the intention is, but I am inclined to think that the point taken by the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) is correct, that there is no provision as to what is to become of the road. When the receivership ends it goes into the hands of the Grand Trunk Company, and we are the Grand Trunk Company. Is it intended to be continued that way and not merged with the Canadian National even after the committee of management is at an end?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is intended that the Grand Trunk system, which includes the Grand Trunk Pacific, be merged in the Canadian National system under one control.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is it so stated in this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think there is any specific provision in the Bill, but the moment the Government gets into the shoes of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk then it may exercise any powers that those shareholders previously exercised. The Government will then be in a position to appoint a manager of the Grand Trunk system, and I presume they will do just what they did in appointing a manager of the Intercolonial to succeed the previous manager. The Government would appoint the Canadian National Board of Directors to administer the Grand Trunk under its

authority as owner of the Grand Trunk stock.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Did we not by legislation specifically transfer the management of the Intercolonial to the Canadian National? I think we did, and I do not think we are doing it in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not think we did. I do not speak with absolute certainty in answer to the hon. member on that point. It may be possible that we did later on in the Canadian National Railway Bill, but previously to that the management of that road was transferred by Order in Council simply as an Act of the Government which owned the road. It was placed under the management of the Canadian National railway just under'the same authority as the Government would exercise in appointing Mr. Gutelius or Mr. Brady or any one else to manage the road.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: After the receivership is at an end what will be the position of the branch lines companies and what will he the responsibility of a province in respect of its guarantee on their bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That matter was specially called to my attention by the member for Kindersley yesterday. The answer is that they are just in the same legal position precisely after as before. We are simply stockholders of the parent company. The branch lines bear the same relation to that company, to their own bondholders and the guarantors, he they a province or private persons, afterwards as before.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The province of Saskatchewan has made a payment of interest oh some of these bonds. When this matter is concluded will this Government make good that payment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My information is that the provinces made some payments in answer to their responsibility as guarantors on some of the bonds. When the Government becomes owner of The road it does not pay the debts of the road; the road pays its own- debts. It has happened in the past, and it may happen in the future, that if the road is not able to secure capital or money with which to take care of its obligations the money may be loaned by the Government under the authority of Parliament. It is expected that the Grand Trunk Company will take care of its obligations afterwards, including the obligation to which the hon. gentleman refers, even though it may be necessary to borrow
money from the Government for the purpose.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do recall something of the incident to which the hon. gentjeman refers, but I think it was the Grand Trunk Pacific that held this stock in the Edmonton Bulletin, either directly or through the medium of a third party. Of course, if that stock is still in the same position it will be the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Government being the owners of the stock of the Grand Trunk, of which the Grand Trunk Pacific is a subsidiary, I suppose it would be in the highly desirable position of being the equitable owners of that asset.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: At the present moment, if the Grand Trunk desired to amalgamate with the Canadian National railways, would it be in a position to do so without the authority of Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Government is not in any way changing the standing of the company, which is still the Grand Trunk Company. The Canadian National railways have power to acquire any other railway in Canada, but that would not give the Grand Trunk Company the right to sell out to the Canadian National or amalgamate with them without some authority from Parliament. If the authority is not given in this Bill, where will it lie?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But suppose they pooled' all their receipts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I presume they could put their receipts where they liked, but the supposition is monstrous. They would not put their receipts, if they were a

private company, into a separate company but into their own treasury. They could divert them from their own treasury if they were mad enough to do so. We are simply, as stockholders of the Grand Trunk, in control of the company. Exercising that control, we appoint the *Canadian National railway director and manager of the Grand Trunk business.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the receipts of each of these companies be kept separately?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not feel that I can answer that question finally. I would presume that there would be separate accounting for the Grand Trunk and the other roads. There is separate accounting now on the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern. When the Grand Trunk comes in even though there is a merger, separate accounting, I think, will continue.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister tells us
that when the receivership of the Grand Trunk Pacific is over the company will be back where it was before the order putting into the hands of the receiver wras made. The financial ability of the company will be no better after the receivership is cancelled than before. The obligations of the company are still outstanding and it is *open to any of the creditors to put it in the hands of a receiver again. What steps do the Government intend to take to secure the road and the physical assets of the company? No doubt they propose to take over the road and operate it. What means are they going to take to prevent an occurrence of that kind? If we do not pay the obligations against the road we cannot stand in the way of any person who seeks to enforce his. rights against the physical assets -of the company. There are bondholders and, I suppose these bonds are secured by a mortgage. They can foreclose their mortgage and to prevent that we will have to pay the bonds. Those who have claims can apply to a judge to have the company put into liquidation. I presume the Government have considered all these matters and have devised means of dealing with eventualities of that kind. Will the minister explain to the committee what course they propose to take in order to hold the company and at the same time pay off, or arrange the claims against the road.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
When the Canadian
National railways are called upon by appointment to administer the Grand Trunk in unison and harmony with the Canadian National system, any portion of that system

has to be protected in its obligations to bondholders or others. It would be protected by the Canadian National management and no doubt when it undertakes the Grand Trunk Pacific it will be done in just the same way as all the component parts of the Canadian National system are protected. We will inquire for a moment how this is done to-day. On the Canadian Northern Ontario, or the Canadian Northern Quebec whose stock is owned by the Canadian Northern, and which in turn is operated by the Canadian National railways, an obligation falls due. If there is no money in the treasury of the Canadian Northern Ontario to discharge that obligation it is lent by the Canadian Northern. A similar process would, I presume, go on in connection with an obligation of the Grand Trunk Pacific. If the money were not there it would be loaned by the parent concern. It is hoped that by means of the advantages of the merger, we may not be far from the day when the revenues will take care of these obligations. It may be that one would fall behind but another would go ahead and as the receipts of all are finally pooled, although separate accounting takes place, there will be money enough, it is hoped, in the treasury, to take care of these separate and individual obligations. But in the meantime a loan will be made out of the common pool to an individual concern to take care of the obligations. If the common pool does not contain sufficient money for that purpose it will then be for the Canadian National railways to secure the funds. They may secure that by a loan from outside in the same way that any other railway does or they may come to the Government for a loan. The Government could not make it, of cou'rse, except under the authority of Parliament. I understand that the Canadian National railways have made loans outside. They have borrowed money outside and the new road may do the same. It will be managed just the same as any other road. If necessary and if Parliament grants it, a government guarantee can be given to the bonds of-the system. I hope I have made it clear to the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It is clear enough to me but I am not satisfied that the Grand Trunk Pacific is good value for the Canadian people to take with its present obligations. I am afraid we are taking too many obligations in connection with this property and that the property is not worth it. The other day we heard from the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) who is a

railway expert that the $280,000,000 which is said to have gone into the Grand Trunk Pacific never went into that road. He takes the responsibility of saying that. I do not know; I am simply quoting his words. We are taking over the road subject to all these liabilities and the minister hopes that the operation of the road will provide for them. If not the main reservoir, which is the treasury of Canada, will have to be called upon to pay the shortage. If the road itself will not pay we will have to pay the obligations out of the revenues of Canada, because we own it. It does not make any difference what the minister says about companies and owning it under different names; when it comes down to the last analysis and money is wanted, it has to come from the treasury of Canada. It is of the highest importance that the people of Canada should know whether they are paying too much for the road and whether they are assuming too gTeat a liability in connection with it. It has had to go to the hands of a receiver because its obligations are too high and its income is too small. I cannot see any good reason to think that the sledding is going to be any better after the receivership is closed out than it was before. I would think that to allow the receivership to take its course would be the safer proposition for the people of Canada. Then it would be stripped of everything about it, the claims could not be satisfied out of the treasury itself and we could certainly afford to buy it better than anybody else.
It would not pay anybody else to buy-at least we would have the advantage over everybody else in buying-and as a business proposition, to a person like myself who has no feeling or sentiment in the matter at all, and perhaps no great responsibility, it would appear that we should get the property for what it is worth-stripped of all the obligations that are against it-which I regard as superfluous obligations, and obligations that are greater than the intrinsic value of that property. If the minister satisfies us, or satisfies the country, he is getting good value and that taking over this property and assuming the liabilities is a good business transaction we have nothing to find fault with; but our experience in connection with this road is that it was not built to weather the storm -it went under because it'was top heavy, it was laden with liabilities, and its earnings were not sufficient to meet the necessary demands. Now if we are going to take over that road would it not be good business
to strip it of those superfluous liabilities, get it down to real running weight, and have nothing to pay but what the road would ordinarily have to pay and what would be a fair liability upon its true and proper capital value.	'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Trunk is not liable at all. If we start the stripping process, who loses first? Who are we stripping in order that we may protect the people of Canada? We are stripping ourselves. The first things to topple over are the loans that we ourselves made. We are the losers; naturally we lose the whole amount that we have been advancing year after year for that line.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If we do, under our first mortgage do we not have the property?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Now the hon. gentleman says: "Let it go to wreck and 'buy in under the first mortgage." Well, of course, the second mortgagees would have something to say about that, and I do not think anybody would suggest that it is not worth-if we can get the Grand Trunk and have a railway system-a good deal more than the first mortgage anyway. But suppose it is not worth the amount of the second mortgage? Suppose it is not worth the total amount of the mortgages-that is the total of the first and second mortgages and the total of the mortgage in .respect of which we and the Grand Trunk are liable? Are we going to be the losers by the policy of the Government now embodied in this Bill? No. All we have to do is to show that to the board of arbitrators and to the extent to which that road is not worth the sum of the first and second mortgages-the Government's mortgages and the Grand Trunk's mortgages-and the joint mortgages, to that extent the Grand Trunk's obligations to the Grand Trunk Pacific are a liability, and the amount of that liability comes off the value of the Grand Trunk's stock. In a word, we are saving ourselves.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is a very indirect way of doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I know it is an indirect way, but it is the only way in the world to do it. Now let me repeat my statement, because this is really very important, and I am anxious that hon. members should fully understand it-that is, if they agree that I am right. Anyway, we are not dictating to the arbitrators at all, any more than we do in all our expropriation legislation; it is for the arbitrators to say what is the business value of the Grand Trunk Pacific road.
Taking everything into account, what is its business value? Do not tell us that its business value is what it cost or what it would take to replace it to-day, because perhaps it should not have been built at all. Take everything into account; determine what its fair value is as a going con-

cern. Having done that, add the total responsibilities until you get to the end of the Grand Trunk responsibilities; then take the difference between the two. That difference represents the net liability of the Grand Trunk and should come out of the value of their stocks. So that we are saving ourselves in relation (to the Grand Trunk Pacific by a charge against the inherent value of the parent company's stocks. That is the very essence of this policy: first of all, a desire to have a real Government system that ought to pay if it does not pay; second, a desire to save to the greatest extent that we can whatever asset the country may have in the Grand Trunk Pacific by charging our loss against the value of the stocks of the parent company, the Grand Trunk.

speechtext:
As regards the termination of receivership, I think it is proper to point out that there is amongst some per sons in the country a misunderstanding regarding the meaning of the words " receivership '' and "liquidation." This agreement being of such great importance must go, not only before lawyers and businessmen accus-

tomed to transactions like this, but before all the people of the country who must be satisfied in regard to it. I find that some people, especially those who are timid about entering upon a policy of government ownership, do not understand the meaning of these words " receivership " and liquidation." They are pleasant, sibilant words, and people not having been accustomed to them before and these words being suddenly thrust into this debate, there is being attached to them by some people an importance which should not be. The leader of the Opposition said in one of his speeches during the course of this debate: Why not liquidate? or words to that effect. Why not continue the receivership? It seems to m.e important that the country should understand that a receivership must be only a temporary holding. When a man has a debt against another man, he has ways of collecting it; or if he has a mortgage securing bonds, he has ways of collecting it. One of those is to get a judgment against the debtor and then issue execution to the sheriff and sell the property. But if it is not advisable to bring a property to auction by public auction, then it is proper that a receiver should be appointed to collect the revenues and prudently to make expenditures and so on. That, however, is only a temporary expedient; you cannot continue a receivership except for a very ordinary length of time. Therefore, a receivership which sounds so pleasant and easy, ig really only something that can be contemplated to last for a time. As regards the word "liquidation," I find some people say: Let us liquidate. That sounds well. They do not seem to understand that the word " liquidation " has a very serious meaning, different from the way in which it sounds. I am speaking now, not for the expert, but for the ordinary everyday citizen who is not accustomed to these transactions. Liquidation means; as the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) has said, that you strip off all the debts; but liquidation in the law means only one thing, that you bring the property to sale by public auction, and in that case you have free competition by rivals for this system and a sale which cannot be brought about by any private arrangement whatever. Therefore, it seems to me that the only possible way to make a good bargain here is by the arrangement which it is attempted by this Bill to carry out, instead of bringing the matter to an auction which must be fair, open, and above board by the courts, which would allow American companies or the Canadian Pacific or any other large
concern to come in and bid, and which would then force the Government to come to the auction with millions of money in its hand which would necessitate another loan. It should be well understood that liquidation means public auction under the hammer, with no secret arrangement whatever. Unless the country is prepared to put up millions of money to equip the Government to go to that auction and buy, the only possible solution is to enter into this arrangement by which they will not have to put up a dollar, but only by good business methods, linking this road up with the present system, will have to endeavour to meet the interest on these bonds and earn the balance for the public treasury.

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I have been anxious
to know what kind of a bargain the Canadian people are making in connection with this road, and that is why I am inquiring as to the liabilitites of this road and what we are paying for it. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) seems to think that liquidation is a frightful thing, an awful thing. Has the hon. gentleman ever heard of a man making an assignment? I am sure in the great metropolis in which -he lives he has heard of men being obliged to make an assignment. After they made an assignment, the assignee would have to sell the property whatever it was, get the most money he could and divide that amongst the creditors. A receiver does the same thing if he does his duty. That is all that this means. A receiver and an assignee are as close together as any two could be. The duty of both would be to get the best possible value for the goods which they hold in trust for the benefit of the creditors and divide that money between them. That is the only way that is known to the commercial world of dealing with a man who goes into insolvency, and to all intents and purposes a single person with a .mortal body and a living soul- is, so far as money is concerned, put into the same category as a corporation. When a corporation gets into deep water, it gets into the hands of a receiver; or it could make an assignment just like an individual, and then the assignee could deal with the goods. Why should we be frightened into paying ten times its value for a piece of property on which we have a mortgage? That is something I cannot understand and which I believe the Canadian' people cannot understand. We are told that the liquidator can hold the property only for a certain time. That is true, but after thatjime he should sell it and get the money for it. Why

should we huy another road when we are told we already have too many railroads? We are told we have two roads now through to the coast where one is enough. Why should we be afraid to sell one of them? Why should this House jump headlong into paying ten prices for a road when we have one too many already and when we could sell this road to-morrow and still leave us with transportation facilities adequate for the needs of the country? I do not think it is good reasoning, good law, or good logic that my hon. friend (Mr. Mowat) gives us when he says we must hang on to this road and pay any price for it lest it may go under the hammer. If a man has two horses and has use for only one, he is not going to be frightened to sell the other one. That is the case with these railroads. We have been told repeatedly that one of our roads, together with the Canadian Pacific, would be sufficient, for our needs. Then why should we not sell the other and get the money for it, instead of dragging it along in this way and taking millions upon millions of dollars every year out of the pockets of the Canadian people to look after it? We are paying for a toy that does not pay and will not pay for many years to come.
Mr. MORPHY;: Which road would the hon. member sell?

speechtext: The one that is now in the hands of a receiver.

speechtext: Which one is that?

subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Grand Trunk
Pacific. We should get it for something like what it is worth. It is idle to say that we should go to these 'arbitrators and get them to put a value upon the equity of redemption under these mortgages. Any lawyer or business man knows that- the only way you can get at the value of the equity of redemption is to put up the property for sale and let the public say what it is woTth. The obligations are paid out of the purchase price, and the balance goes as the equity of redemption to the man who mortgaged this property. The position we are getting ourselves into is that of a mortgagee in possession. I do not know whether the Minister of Railways is sufficient of a lawyer to know what is the position of a mortgagee in possession. It means that he is in possession of a property which ^ he has taken as security, but the title is not altogether in him because the equity of redemption is still outstanding. He must strictly account to the owner of the property for every cent the property earns and for 
every advantage he has derived from it. The only thing for a mortgagee in possession to do is to foreclose and let the property be sold for what it will bring. If he wants the title himself he must pay what the public thinks the property is worth, but if somebody else bids higher and gets the property, the mortgagee gets back the interest he had in the property. I say it is not good business to take over this property or any other property and assume liabilities which are possibly twice its value.
I protest on behalf of the people of this country against this transaction for the reason that we are assuming altogether too much liability, and undertaking to pay too much money for the property when we could get it for wihat it is worth stripped of all these bonds and mortgages and stocks. We could buy the property for what the public says it is worth at public auction. That is the position I take, straight and clear, and if it is not understood the fault is not mine. If the Government makes a bad bargain they make it in the face of the warning I am giving them that they are paying too much for this property. The Minister of the Interior said 'himself, not half an hour ago, that he knew the property was not worth the claims against it. He would not undertake to say what proportion of the claims it was worth, but takes this property holus bolus and assumes all responsibility in regard to it. There should be some remedy by which we could get clear of assuming obligations that are altogether too great in connection with a piece of property that we could very well do without.
