subtopic: BILD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If a man has a first and third mortgage on a house and he wants to get title, his proper course would be to foreclose the first mortgage and put the house up for sale. It may not sell for enough to pay the first mortgage. If so, he has the house, and having the house, what is the use of his bothering about the third mortgage? The only good there was in that mortgage lay in the fact that it was binding on the house, but as the house is his property on the foreclosure of the first mortgage the third mortgage represents nothing to him. We could get title to the road on our first mortgage, and the arbitrators need not be befogged by considerations of the second mortgage.

of value. I cannot see any object in foreclosing in order to get title, because we virtually have it now. The stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company belongs to us and we have title by virtue of that ownership.

speechtext: Before the question is answered, and to illustrate very briefly the point which has been raised, I would like to relate an incident that occurred yesterday. speechtext:
It is well to direct the attention of the committee and the country to the fact that the Minister of Railways, when he brings down this important piece of legislation, is not aware of the expenditure he will have to meet in connection with the terminal facilities in Toronto and Montreal.
My information is that the Grand Trunk itself will have to pay some $30,000,000 for terminal facilities in Toronto, and that the changes in the Grand Trunk terminal
[Mr. Vien.J
facilities in Montreal will involve another expenditure of over $50,000,000. This, added to the amount which will be involved in bringing the physical condition of the road up to normal, as suggested by the Drayton-Acworth report, will mean a necessary expenditure of over $150,000,000.	$51,000,000
necessary according to the Drayton-Acworth report three years ago; $50,000,000 necessary for the elevation of the Grand Trunk from Point St. Charles to Bonaventure station and the erection of a new station there, and $30,000,000 for terminal facilities. The Minister of Railways comes to this House and gives all the information that he has in his possession, but he has to admit that, before entering into such an agreement, before asking Parliament to enact such legislation as this; he is not aware of the amount which will be involved in those terminal facilities. The House and the country have a right to be better informed before they are asked to pass such legislation. When .a man buys a house or an ordinary business plant, such as a shop, or shares in an industrial company, what is he going to do before he takes any steps towards entering N into an agreement? He will inquire first as ,to the physical condition of the plant, the financial standing of the company, the debenture indebtedness of the company p and only when he is in full possession of those facts, will he draw up the agreement or will he discuss the various terms of it. In the present instance nothing of that kind has been done. The minister, with candour, maybe to his credit, but with an ignorance which is hardly creditable, tells us that he does not know the amount involved in those terminal facilities. Yet he is willing to assume the responsibility of taking over the road. If the information that I have is accurate, to the $501,000,000 of a liability that the country will be saddled with according to the statement of the minister, we shall also find ourselves saddled with $150,000,000 of additional expenditure just for these terminal facilities. The minister says: But this will be saved; we must have terminal facilities in Toronto; we must have terminal facilities in Montreal; we are combining all the railways, and this is one additional reason why the Government should take over the Grand Trunk railway. His argument is absolutely wrong. The terminals in Montreal will be put under a union plan, all the railways now using Bonaventure station will have to use the new terminals. Whether we buy the Grand Trunk or not, the Intercolonial and the Canadian Govern-

ment railways will have an opportunity of using the terminals in Montreal. In Toronto the same thing is true. There is already a terminal company organized to build terminals in Toronto, so that it will afford no advantage whatever to the Government or to the Government railways to take over the Grand Trunk. But the House, before it is called upon to sanction such legislation, should know the full extent of the liability that the country is being asked to assume. It is putting the country under a false impression when we say that the physical condition of the road is good and satisfactory, when, as a matter of fact, over $150,000,000 must be expended before the road will be in a normal condition. Yet the Minister of Railways tells us that he is satisfied with the physical condition of the road. He tells us that he has the information; that he has travelled over the road, and that he has a personal knowledge that the road is in a good condition. Notwithstanding that, he is obliged to make the admission that he does not know the amount of expenditure that the Government will have to make for these terminal facilities. How can the minister reconcile the statement that he does not know the amount of expenditure involved in the terminal facilities with his statement of a few moments ago that he is satisfied with the physical condition of the road? I hardly see how the minister can reconcile these two statements, and he should put before the House all the facts, so that the country may know that in buying this railway, it will have to make an expenditure of $150,000,000 for terminal facilities in Montreal and Toronto and for betterments of the road which have been neglected for a few years.
